Confirmation Tests for HIV 
*199. SHRI ANANTRAY DEVSHANKER DAVE: Will the Minister of 
HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) which are the tests required to be conduced for confirmation of HIV; 
(b) whether tests for HIV confirmation are different for children less than, 
two years; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; 
(d) whether HIV testing machines are available in the Medical Colleges; 
 
58 

[3 December, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
(e) whether these Colleges are authorised to announce the status of an AIDS 
victim; and 
(f) if so, the number of cases detected till date? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. C.P. 
THAKUR): (a) There are various tests available for confirmation of HIV based on 
the detection of antibodies and virus particles. These tests are : (I) Enzyme Linked 
Immunosorbent Assays [ELISA]; (2) Rapid HIV tests; (3) Western Blot [WB]; (4) 
Indirect fluorescent antibody test [IFA]; and (5) Polymerase Chain Reaction 
[PCR] for detecting virus particles. 
Under the National AIDS Control Programme, ELISA and Rapid HIV Assays are 
being used for diagnosis of HIV infected persons, asymptomatic HIV persons and 
epidemiological surveillance. 
(b) and (c) Yes, Sir. The HIV status of children below the age of 2 years can be 
detected by a test known as Polymerase Chain reaction. Children have passive 
antibodies from HIV infected mothers which may not reveal the true HIV status of 
the child. These antibodies disappear around 18 months of age when sero 
conversion takes place. Thereafter, HIV can be detected by conventional tests. 
(d) to (f) Yes, Sir. In children below 18 months of age, it is advised to conduct 
PCR test to detect the HIV particles. HIV testing machines, for detecting 
antibodies i.e. ELISA readers are available in a majority of Public Sector Medical 
Colleges; the machines for conducting the polymerase Chain Reaction [PCR] test 
are available at a few centers only, and are not recommended for routine diagnostic 
use. The Medical Colleges are authorized to reveal the status to the HIV/AIDS 
victim only, after pre and post test counseling, and maintaining full confidentiality. 
The cumulative number of AIDS cases, including children, reported till 31st 
October, 2001 is 29007.

Statement 
Small Family Norms 
(1) Panchayats and Zila Parishads will be rewarded and honoured for

achieving reductions in infant mortality and birth rates and promoting 
literacy with completion of primary schooling.

birth order 1 or 2.

will continue. A cash incentive of Rs. 500 is awarded to mothers who 
have their first child after 19 years of age, for birth of the first or second

compliance with antenatal check up, institutional delivery by trained 
birth attendant, registration of birth and BCG immunisation.

personal accident insurance cover for the spouse undergoing sterilisation.

00 The Government has taken following actions in the context of the present 
international scenario; 
1. A detailed list of biological agents used as weapons prepared by the 
Indian Council of Medical Research along with signs and symptoms, 
likely method of dissemination, incubation period, lethality and the 
availability of vaccines, anti-microbial therapy and treatment has been 
circulated to Health Secretary and Di rector of Health Services of all 
States/UTs., and Central Govt, hospitals advising them to take 
following precautionary steps. 
* Earmarking of maximum number of beds for emergency contingency 
* Stocking of vaccines/sera/drugs to the extent possible. 
* Setting up a special team of doctors for coordinated action. They should 
be sensitized on the impact of such weapons and treatment measures. 
114 

[3 December, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
Z Two expert group meetings were held (1st & 17th October) in the 
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare to review the management 
(diagnosis, treatment, IEC activities etc.) of recently emerging diseases 
of public health importance like Dengue, Anthrax etc. Eminent experts 
in the field of medical science from different organizations in the 
country, senior officials of Ministry of Health & F.W., and chiefs of 
different Government and private hospitals in Delhi participated in the 
meeting and deliberated on various aspects of the bio-terrorism in the 
backdrop of the current global situation. 
3. Two expert group meetings (18th and 21 st October, 2001) were held to 
finalise guidelines to be issued in CD Alert. 
4. National Institute of Communicable Diseases, 22, Sham Nath Marg, 
Delhi-110054, an Institute under Directorate General of Health Services 
has been designated as the nodal ag ency for carrying out the tests of 
suspected Anthrax samples. Around the clock control room is 
functioning Telephone Nos. 3912901 (Between 10.00 A.M. to 6.00 P.M.) 
& 3971875 (Between 6.00 P.M. to 10.00 A.M.) to receive and test the 
suspected samples. Till the evening of 27th November, 2001, 322 
suspected envelopes were received in the NICD for testing. 303 samples 
have already been tested, none was found positive. 
5. CD Alert, a monthly Newsletter of National Institute of Communicable 
Diseases titled "Bioterrorism-Public Health system to Remain Alert" 
exclusively on Anthrax has been wide ly circulated. It has also been 
put in the Website of MOHFW (http:/mohfw.nic.in) for information 
of general public. 
6. Do's & Don'ts has already been published in the leading National Dailies 
regarding Anthrax. 
7. A meeting-cum workshop on Biological & Chemical Terrorism was 
convened by the Department of Health on 29th October, 2001 in New 
Delhi wherein Health Secretary, Home Secretary and Director of Health 
Services from various States/UTs., eminent experts in the field of 
medical science from different organizations in the country and heads 
of different hospitals in Govt, and private sector in Delhi participated 
and deliberated on various aspects. The representatives from the States 
informed the preparatory measures taken by them and assured 
availability of drugs in adequate quantity to tackle any situation.

Statement I 
Initiatives taken in consultation with the states for containing the growth of 
population and expediting the pace of implementation of National Family 
Welfare Programme: 
Stabilizing population 
• An Empowered Action Group has been constituted under me chairmanship 
of the Union Health and Family Welfare Minister for focussed attention on 
132 

[3 December, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
improving the coverage and outreach of services in the eight states of Uttar 
Pradesh, Uttaranchal, Bihar, Jharkhand, Rajasthan, Orissa, Madhya Pradesh 
and Chhattisgarh, involving voluntary associations, community organizations 
and Panchayati Raj institutions in mis national effort. 
• In the order to arrest the adverse sex ratio, an intensive campaign has 
been launched against the practice of female foeticide through the 
mass media, print and electronic media as well as through the voluntary 
organizations for stricter enforcem ent of the Law i.e. the Pre-Natal 
Diagnostic Techniques (Regulation and Prevention of Misuse) Act, 
1994. A meeting of all Appropriate Authorities appointed in the States 
for implementation of provisions of the Act has been held for more 
vigorous implementation. 
• Male participation in the programme has increased manifold with the 
growing popularity ofNo Scalpel Vasectomy—a much-improved method. 
Upgradation of health Infrastructure 
• The Prime Minister's Gramodaya Yo jana has provided in the years 
2000-01 and 2001-02 central alloca tion of Rs. 809 crores for the 
maintenance and upkeep of primary health infrastructure in rural India. 
• Area specific projects have been taken up for strengthening primary 
health care services in the states of Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Orissa, 
Maharashtra, Gujarat and Kerala under Integrated Population 
Development (IPD) Project supported by UNFPA, for slums in cities/ 
towns in the states of Andhra Pr adesh, Karnataka and West Bengal 
in World Bank supported IPP VIII project, in Assam and Karnataka 
IPPIX project, in 33 districts of U.P. under IFPS project supported by 
USAID and in Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra and other demographically 
deficient areas under various programmes with the assistance of 
DANIDA, DFID and World Bank. 
• Norms for payment for items like rent , contigencies, stipend etc. for 
family welfare infrastructure units set up in the States/UTs over the 
past several years have been revised. 
• In order to strengthen the availability of health staff steps have been 
taken for development of cadre of Nurse Midwives in public and private 
133 

RAJYA SABHA [3 December, 2001 ] 
sector, contractual appointments of ANMs, Public Health Nurses and 
Laboratory Technicians. Private Doctors and Anesthetists are being 
engaged on per visit payment basis. 
Integrated service delivery: Reproductive health 
• Immunization is key to health of children by reducing infant mortality, 
RCH outreach services such as immunization, ante and post natal 
check ups, information and conselling, as well a contraceptive services 
are being provided. This scheme which covered 50 districts last year, 
has been extended during the current year to 101 additional districts. 
• In an effort to supplement existing interventions seeking to expand 
outreach and coverage, a series of Parivar Kalyan and Swasthya Melas 
have been held all over the country including Mathura, Delhi, Lucknow, 
Kargil, Patna, Badal, Perambur, Sultanpur (U.P.) and Ghazipur (U.P.). 
Many more are being planned as a chain of the regular process. 
• RCH Campus are also periodically organised at primary health centres 
for providing integrated services to the rural population, especially 
women and children, in remote and under-served areas. The scheme, 
which was started in 101 districts last year, has now been extended to 
77 additional districts in the current year. 
• The programme for training of traditional birth attendants (Dais), 
with provision of kits, has been introduced in 142 districts having 
less than 30% safe deliveries. 
Statement II 
Fourteen National Socio-Demographic Goals for 2010 enumerated in the 
The National Population Policy, 2000 
1) Address the unmet needs for basic reproductive and child health services, 
supplies and infrastructure. 
2) Make school education up to age 14 free and compulsory, and reduce 
dropouts at primary and secondary school levels to below 20 percent for 
both boys and girls. 
3) Reduce infant mortality rate to below 30 per 1 OOv live births. 
134 

[3 December, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
4) Reduce maternal mortality rate to below 100 per 100,000 live births. 
5) Achieve universal immunization of children against all vaccine preventable 
diseases. 
6) Promote delayed marriage for girls, not earlier than age 18 and preferably 
after 20 years of age. 
7) Achieve 80 percent institutional deliveries and 100 percent deliveries by 
trained persons. 
8) Achieve universal access to information/counseling and services for fertility 
regulation and contraception with a wide basket of choices. 
9) Achieve 100 per cent registration of births, deaths, marriage and pregnancy. 
 
10) Contain the spread of Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome (AIDS), 
and promote greater integration between the management of reproductive 
tract infection (RTI) and sexually tr ansmitted infractions (STI) and the 
National AIDS Control Organisation. 
11) Prevent and control communicable diseases. 
12) Integrate Indian System of Medicines (ISM) in the provision of 
reproductive and child health services, and in reaching out to households. 
13) Promote vigorously the small family norm to achieve replacement levels 
of total fertility rate (TFR) of 2.1. 
14) Bring about convergence in implementation of related social sector 
programmes so that family welfare becomes a people centered programme.

1423. SHRI SURESH PACHOURI: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have stopped the practice of setting targets for 
important family welfare programmes; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(c) how Government propose to improve performance of family welfare 
programmes, especially in BIMARU States? 
145 

RAJYA SABHA [3 December, 2001 ] 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. C. P. THAKUR): 
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Upto 31st March, 1996, the achievements of Family Welfare Programme 
were assessed on the basis of the targets given from above for individual 
contraceptives. This led to a situation where the achievements of contraceptives 
targets had become ends in themselves. This target, system was started with the 
concepts that the achievement of contraceptive target would definitely lead to 
decrease in birth rate and subsequently in decrease in population. However, over 
the years it was realized that in the target system there were many drawbacks. 
For instance, users preference in choosing contraceptive was not reflected: due 
to non-availability of required contracep tives for the users, targets were not 
realized; there was no system of feed back on contraceptives needs- of users and 
thus the quality of services to the beneficiaries did not receive due attention. 
(c) Currently, six Area Projects are bein g implemented in the selected 
Districts/Cities of 13 States including Delhi at a total cost of Rs. 1194.78 crores 
with the financial assistance from World Bank, DANIDA, DFID (UK), UNFPA 
and German Government. In addition, under the World Bank Assisted RCH 
programme, 24 RCH Sub-project (17 Districts and 7 Cities) are under 
implementation in 17 States at a total co st of Rs. 283.88 crores for a period of 
five years since October, 1997. 
The National Population Policy, 2000 adopted by the Government in 
February, 2000 envisages strengthening and energizing the Family Welfare 
services in the four States of Bihar, M.P., Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh including 
all other States. 
An Empowered Action Group has been constituted within the Ministry of 
Health and Family Welfare, for preparing area specific programmes with special 
emphasis on States including these States, which are lagging behind in 
population control.

Ethical Guidelines on Bio-Medical Research 
1426.     SHRI N. K. PREMACHANDRAN: 
     SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNTIA:  
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the recent trials on human subjects of 
an anti-cancer drug in Regional Cancer Centre at Thiruvananthapuram without 
following the rules properly; 
(b) if so, whether any probe has been conducted into the incident; 
(c) if so, the outcome of the same; 
(d) whether Government propose to give interim relief to the victims; if 
not, the reasons therefor; 
(e) whether Government propose to issue certain ethical guidelines on bio-
medical research to avoid such incidents in future; 
(f) if so, the details thereof; and 
(g) the fresh steps taken to make rule s relating to clearance for clinical 
trials more stringent? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. C. P. 
THAKUR):(a)Yes,sir. 
(b) to (d) A team constituted by the Central Government has investigated the 
alleged use of banned drug on cancer patients at Regional Cancer Centre, 
Thiruvananthapuram. The Central team observed that though violation of human 
rights or use of banned drug was not involved in the trial, however, there have 
been lapses in respect of the regulatory procedure required to be followed for 
conducting such trials in the country. 
Regional Cancer Centre, Thiruvananthapuram has been served a show cause 
notice and advised to suspend all ongoing clinical trials with drugs for a period of six 
months. They have also been advised to obtain all necessary approvals from the 
government and revise the list of ethical committee members of the centre. 
In view of above, the question of giving interim relief does not arise. 
(e) and (f) Indian Council of Medi cal Research (ICMR), New Delhi has 
published "Ethical Guidelines for Bio-medical Research on human Subject" which 
will be followed by all researchers/institutions engaged in bio-medical research 
in the country.

Casualties due to overdose of Vitamin-A in Nagaon District 
1428. DR. ARUN KUMAR SARMA: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of the casualties due to overdose of Vitamin-A in Nagaon 
district of Assam on 12th November, 2001 during administration of UNICEF 
sponsored vaccine as well as food poisoning cases due to intake of pulses in 
various parts of Assam during the last six months; and 
(b) the lives lost and suffered, causes detected and responsibilities fixed for 
such incidents alongwith date and location-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. C.P. 
THAKUR): (a) and (b) As per information furnished by the State Government 
of Assam after the recent Vitamin A ca mpaign 689 children were treated for 
minor illnesses without hospitalization; 41 were hospitalized and released after 
recovery; and 5 children are redported to have died in Nagaon district. Four 
out of the five children who died did not receive Vitamin A. The remaining 
child was suffering from fever for one week prior to death. 
After consuming soaked gram on 10th August 2001 after a peace rally held 
the day earlier, 1819 children suffered from diarrhoea and vomiting in Barpeta 
district. Of these two died. 230 students and 44 members of the staff suffered 
from food poisoning in Assam Valley School in Sonitpur district on 7.9.2001. 
470 people attending the Flag Hoisting ceremony at Banbari Mini Stadium in 
Nalbari district on 15th August 2001 suffered food poisoning on 16th August 
2001. One death is reported. 60 cases of food poisoning were reported from 
village Niz-Sipajhar in Darrang district after consuming Prasad of 'Matimah' on 
17.9.2001. Kamrup district reported 11 cases of food poisoning from Rangia. In 
the same district 17 students of Kachari Basti School, Guwahati suffered food 
poisoning on 5.9.2001. 
The State Government has collected samples of pulses and water from the 
affected districts. Some samples of pulses were found to contain 
organophosphorus and some samples of water were found to be contaminated 
with coliform organisms. Free medical treatment was provided to the affected 
people. Bakeries have been instructed to sell fresh and quality products only. 
The district authorities stopped sale of moog, gram etc., People were advised 
not to consume grams, moogs and their products by circulating leaflets, through 
newspapers and other media.

1446. SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: Will the Minister of LAW, JUSTICE

Executive, whether Government have worked out some mechanism or arrangement 
like Lokpal to work as code of conduct for the Judges so that the members of the 
Judiciary are subject to disciplinary and Conduct Rules framed by the State 
Governments and the High Courts? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW, JUSTICE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI 
ARUN JAITLEY): The issue of Judicial  Accountability was discussed at the 
Conference of Chief Justices held in 1990 and on the basis of the broad consensus 
emerging out of the deliberations, the Chief Justice of India summed up the 
position as follows: 
"The Chief Justice "Of the High Court has the competence to receive 
complaints against the conduct of the Judges of his court and when 
he receives any he would look into it for finding out if it deserves to 
be closely looked into. Where he is satisfied that the matter requires 
to be examined, he shall have f acts ascertained in such manner as 
he considers appropriate keeping the nature of allegations in view 
and if he is of the opinion that the matter is such that it.should be 
reported to the Chief Justice of India, he shall do so. 
The Chief Justice of India shall act in a similar manner in regard to 
complaints relating to conduct of Judges of the Supreme Court and 
in regard to conduct of Chief Justices of the High Courts. 
On the basis of the facts ascertain ed, the Chief Justice of the High 
Court or the Supreme Court, as the case may be shall take such 
appropriate action as may be considered proper, keeping the interests 
of the judiciary as the paramount consideration." 
The complaints received against the Judges of the Supreme Court and the 
High Courts are dealt with in the manner indicated above. 
One of the items of the National Agenda for Governance is to set up a 
National Judicial Commission (NJC) to make recommendations for judicial 
appointment in the Supreme Court of India and the High Courts and to draw up 
a Code of Ethics. The Government is committed to the idea of setting up the 
Commission to deal with these matters. 
The subject matter regarding corruption in lower Judiciary is the concern of 
the respective High Court in accordance wi th the provisions of article 235 of 
the Constitution of India.

(Prevention of Atrocities) Rules, 1995 were notified vide No. 145 dated 31.03.1995. 
Rule 3 of the said Rules provide for precautionary and preventive measures which 
provide that the State Government shall take the following measures with a view 
to prevent atrocities on Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes:— 
(i) Identify the area where it has reasons to believe that atrocity may 
take place or there is an apprehension of recurrence of an offence 
under the Act; (ii) Order the District Magistrate and Superintendent 
of Police or any 
other to visit the identified area and review the law and order 
situation; (Hi) If deem necessary, in the identified area, cancel the arms 
licenses of the 
persons, not being members of the Scheduled Castes or the Scheduled 
Tribes, their near relations, servants or employees and family friends and 
get such arms deposited in the Government Armoury; (iv) Seize all 
illegal fire arms and prohibit any illegal manufacture of 
fire arms; (v) With a view to ensure the safety of person and 
property, if deem 
necessary, provide arms licenses to the members of the Scheduled 
Castes and the Scheduled Tribes; (vi) Constitute a high power State-
level committee, district and divisional 
level committees or such number of other committees as deem proper 
and necessary for assisting the Government in implementation of 
the provisions of the Act; (vii) Set-up a vigilance and monitoring 
committee to suggest effective 
measures to implement the provisions of the Act; 
190 

[3 December, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
(viii) Set-up Awareness Centres and organize Workshops in the identified 
area or at some other place to educate the persons belonging to the 
Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes about their rights and 
the protection available to them under the provisions of various Central 
and State enactments or rules, regulations and schemes framed 
thereunder; 
(ix) Encourage Non-Government Organizations for establishing and 
maintaining Awareness Centre and organizing Workshops and 
provide them necessary financial and other sort of assistance; 
(x) Deploy special police force in the identified area; 
(xi) By the end of every quarter, review the law and order situation, 
functioning of different committees, performance of Special Public 
Prosecutors, Investigating Officers and other Officers responsible 
for implementing the provisions of the Act and the cases registered 
under the Act.

laid on the Table of each House of Parliament by the Central Government, in 
accordance with Section 21 (4) of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled 
Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989. The Annual Report for the year 
ended 31.12.1998 has already been laid on the Table of the Rajya Sabha on

Low literacy pockets in tribal areas of Gujarat 
1482. SHRI AHMED PATEL: Will the Minister of TRIBAL AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have identified low literacy pockets in tribal areas 
of Gujarat particularly amongst the tribal girls and women; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the steps Government have taken to spread literacy in such pockets of 
the State? 
THE MINISTER OF TRIBAL AFFAIRS (SHRI JUAL ORAM): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The districts having less than 10% literacy rate among ST women as per 
1991 census have been identified as low literacy pockets in the country. Kutch 
and Banaskantha districts in Gujarat have been so identified. 
(c) A new Scheme of Educational Complex in Low Literacy Pockets for 
Development of Women Literacy in Tribal Areas was introduced in 1993-94 to 
spread literacy in the low literacy pockets so identified. Under the Scheme, as 
many as five complexes have so far been set up for educating the tribal girls in the 
identified low literacy pockets of the State of Gujarat 
Review of Utilization of SCA 
1483. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of TRIBAL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the deviation in the utilization of funds 
under SCA to Tribal Sub-Plan (TSP); 
212 

[3 December, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether Government have conducted any review of the manner of 
utilization of SCA; 
(d) whether Government have deputed any official for the spot verification 
of works; and 
"  (e) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF TRIBAL AFFAIRS (SHRI JUAL ORAM): (a) and (b) In 
the Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India for the year ended 
March, 1998, it has, inter- alia, been brought out that scrutiny of records in 
selected districts of An dhra Pradesh, Assam, Bi har, Himachal Pradesh, 
Jammu & Kashmir, Madhya Pradesh, Manipur, Rajasthan, Sikkim, Tamil Nadu, 
Tripura, West Bengal and Daman & Diu revealed that funds aggregating Rs. 
85.88 crores, which pertain to Special Ce ntral Assistance to Tribal Sub Plan 
were diverted to other schemes/activities. These observations are based on 
sample check of documents for the period 1992-98 of the Ministry and the 
implementing departments and agencies of 17 States and one U.T. The matter 
has been taken up with the State Govts, concerned. 
(c) to (e) Central Government Officer s visit the States/UTs for reviewing 
and ascertaining the progress of implementation of schemes. Meetings/ 
conferences are convened at Central leve l with Ministers in-charge of Tribal 
Welfare of States along with the concerned Secretaries to review physical and 
financial progress of schemes/projects. In addition, the following measures are 
also taken to ensure effective and timely utilization of Central grants under 
SCA: 
(i) Utilisation Certificates are insisted upon as a pre-requisite for further 
release of funds; 
(ii) Periodic progress reports regarding the status of implementation of 
schemes are obtained; 
(iii) At the State level, the agencies like Tribes Advisory Council, Project 
Implementation Committees of ITDPs at Block levels and Panchayat 
Samities monitor timely spending of funds and effective 
implementation of schemes.

Rate of royalty on Crude Oil 
SHRI ANANTRAY DEVSHANKER DAVE (G ujarat): Sir, the rate of 
royalty on crude oil and gas is being fixed by the Central Government and is 
revised from time to time. Initially, the price of indigenous crude oil and royalty 
was determined by the Administered Pricing Mechanism (APM) system. 
The Government of India has now announced the phase-wise 
dismantling of the APM with effect from 01-04-1998 on petroleum products, 
thereby linking the price of  the indigenous crude with that of the international 
price of comparable crude. In the phase dismantling programme, it has been 
accepted, in principle, to value the crude oil produced indigenously at par with 
the prevailing market price in the inte rnational market for comparable crude. 
The Government of India has cons tituted a Committee, under the 
Chairmanship of Joint Secretary (Exploration), Ministry of Petroleum and 
Natural Gas, New Delhi, to decide the rate of royalty payable to the State 
Governments. At present, the ad hoc rate of royalty on crude oil is Rs. 
850/MT with effect from 1.12.1999. 
The Gujarat Government has made several representations to the 
Government of India to increase the royalty rate on crude oil. The salient 
points are as follows: 
1. The royalty rates for the period 1993 to 1998 should be finalised at 
the earliest. Royalty should be based on the intrinsic value of crude 
oil or international price, whichever is higher. Royalty should be fixed 
at the rate of 40 per cent of the selling price. 
2. The State Government has emphasized that the royalty rate beyond 
1.4.1998 should be linked with the in ternational price of comparable 
crude, and the Government of India' s notification for dismantling the 
regime should be enforced in totality, and the ad hoc fixhq of the 
price of crude oil should be done away with.

the period 1993-98 and the new scheme of royalty from 1.4.1998 onwards, 
the State Government is facing a huge monetary loss. ,

Need to establish an Institute of Seismological   Research in Gujarat 
SHRI GOPALSINH G. SOLANKI (Gujarat ): Sir, Gujarat is a State 
which has experienced two major earthquakes of a magnitude of more than 
8.0 on the Richter Scale, and more than twenty earthquakes of a magnitude of 
more than 5.0 on the Richter Scale, from the year 1819 to 2001. I may also 
state that this year also, the State has experienced more than 250 after-
shocks with a magnitude of 3.8 to 4.9, in the region of Kutch and Saurashtra. 
The earthquake of 26 th January, 2001 was the severest, which had damaged 
property worth about Rs. 50,000 cror es, and had taken 12,000 odd lives. The 
Gujarat region, being on seismic line, coul d face more devastations in future 
also, if earthquakes occur again. It cannot be denied that this is because of the 
increasing population density and levelling up of industrial and civil 
infrastructure. Sir, Gujarat does not have any Seismological Research Institute 
to help in such a situation, and save th e people from _the disaster. Therefore, 
it has become a necessity to establish an  Institute of Seismological Research 
in Gujarat so that lives could be saved by studying the intensity of the coming 
earthquake well in advance, and the people could be informed to take 
precautions, and damages could be prevent ed. This institution will be of great 
importance for collecting data from nearby stations and informing the 
predictions, if any, to the people. Besi des, this institute shall not only be 
teaching short-term courses, but shall also  teach up to the level of graduation, 
post-graduation as well as research studies, to about 140 students for which 
Rs. 26 crores, under non-Plan scheme, and Rs. 7 crores, under Plan scheme, 
shall be required. This may please be sanctioned by the Department of 
Science and Technology. Also, this project be permitted to be implemented, in 
consultation with the network of the overseas institutions.   Therefore, I urge

diseases, its recovery rate is only 50 per cent. It is a silent killer. The Hepatitis 
virus attacks the liver, which is an important organ of the body. Hepatitis leads 
to jaundice, cirrhosis or liver cancer. The Hepatitis virus is transmitted through 
contaminated water, infected injectio n needles, unsafe sex, contaminated 
blood, etc. Despite all these things, no vaccine is yet available for Hepatitis -

democracy is of the people, for the pe ople and by the people. To ensure that 
each voter can avail of this fundamental right to vote, the Election Commission 
compiles voters' list from time to time and ensures that these votes are cast. 
For this purpose, it takes the help of  the local administration and the State 
Governments. This is the very foun dation of democracy and requires that 
honesty and impartiality be observed. Unfortunately, this sense of honesty has 
been corrupted. An MP from Rampur, Uttar Pradesh, had recently filed a 
complaint with the Central Election Commission about the major discrepancies 
in the electoral rolls in Thakurdwara Assembly constituency.

15,800 people from the minority community were missing from the rolls, and 
21,000 fictitious names of the majori ty community were incorporated. The 
CEC instructed the State Government to  suspend four senior officials and 
transfer 10 others. It is suspected that the ruling party and the Government of 
Uttar Pradesh intend to use the same tactic in the upcoming elections. Several 
parties have expressed their concern over the legality of the electoral rolls in 
the whole of Uttar Pradesh.

carefully scrutinize the electoral lists to avoid any sort of rigging, reinduct the

This amendment to the Companies Act of 1956 is intended to bring 
about a procedural change in the procedure of buy-back of shares by 
companies themselves. 
Sir, in the year 1999, after in itially it was promulgated as an 
Ordinance, the Companies Amendment Ac t of 1999 was passed by this hon. 
House. That Act had added the provis ion of section 77A, and permitted a 
company to buy-back up to 25 per cent of its share capital. Originally, the 
concept of a company was that a company could never be permitted to buy-
back its own shares. But the corporate governance the world over changed, 
and companies were also permitted to buy-back shares, and in 1999, we 
amended our own Companies Act, enabling our companies to also buy-back 
up to 25 per cent of the company shares . After a buy-back is completed, there 
are two processes the world over, either those shares are kept in treasury for 
being redistributed again in future or those shares are destroyed after the buy-
back itself. We had opted to take the se cond option. Sir, this amendment only 
brings about a procedural change. The procedural change being that whereas 
to permit 25 per cent of the buy-back, a Special Resolution of the AGM or the 
EGM of the company is required for purc hasing up to 10 per cent out of those 
25 per cent of the shares, the pr ocedure has been made simpler. For 
purchase of ten per cent of the shares or buy-back of the ten per cent of the 
shares, the Board of Directors of a company is being empowered. Under the 
corporate governance, there are severa l powers which are there with the 
Annual General Body of the company. There are also powers which are there 
with the management of the company. The second change which has been 
brought about is that a company whic h buys-back its shares, cannot buy-back 
a second tranche within 365 days. Therefore, a one year gap would have to be 
maintained, and thirdly, a company for th e next six months is not permitted to 
make any fresh issue of capital of the shares of the company itself. These are 
the three procedural changes, which have been brought. The object of this is 
to simplify the procedure and enable the compalny to buy-back, because a 
suggestion was made as to how does it help small shareholders and the 
investors as far as the company is concerned. Sir, the object of simplifying the 
buy-back procedure up to ten per cent and enabling the companies to buy-
back, particularly, in a situation

THE INDIAN SUCCESSION (AMENDMENT) BILL, 2001 
THE MINISTER OF LAW, JUSTICE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS 
(SHRI ARUN JAITLEY): Madam Deputy Chairman, I move : 
"That the Bill further to amend the Indian Succession Act, 
I925,be taken into consideration." 
The Indian Succession Act, 1925, was aimed at consolidating the law 
relating to testamentary and intestate su ccession, as was prevalent at that 
time in the country. Chapter II of Part V of this Act mainly deals with intestate 
succession of Christians. There are two pa rticular provisions which this Bill 
seeks to amend. Section 32 of the Act, in this Chapter, recognizes 
288 

[3 December, 2001] RAJYA SABHA  
the Christian widow as one of the successors to succeed to the property of her 
deceased husband. However, there is an Ex planation attached to it, the effect 
of the Explanation is, if, at the time of the marriage, there is an agreement 
between the wife and husband, in that event, the wife, on becoming a widow, 
will be excluded from her husband's succession. Madam, though this was 
originally conceived to be something which would have been opposed to 
public policy, because there was a specific statutory provision in 1925, this has 
been sustained. We have been receivi ng various representat ions that this 
should be done away with from the statute book; and such a provision should 
have no recognition, particularly, in the present age. The Kerala Women's 
Commission and several other non-Governmental organisations and various 
Christian Women's organisations have been representing to the Government 
that this Explanation should be deleted and a Christian widow should be 
entitled to succeed to the property of her husband, particularly, if he dies 
intestate. 
The second provision is with regard to the provisions of Section 213 
of the Indian Succession Act. This is in tended to bring the Christians on par 
with other communities in the country. T he provisions of Section 213 does not 
apply to Muslims. It also doesn't apply to Hindus, Jains and Buddhists, except 
a certain category who live in 3 metropolitan towns. Since there is no demand 
yet in relation to that category of the Hindus, we are not looking into those at 
the moment. But, with regard to Christians, an exception has been made that 
upon the death of a Christian, there is  a probate mandatorily required to be 
obtained by his successors all over the country. This is a long-drawn process 
where Christian heirs have to go to court and spend money on litigation and 
then get the order of the court to enabl e them to succeed to the predecessor 
interests. 
Some months ago, I received a representation signed by Christian 
Members of Parliament belonging to both Houses of Parliament. About 23 
Members wanted a change in this particul ar provision. Thereafter, I consulted 
various other Christian organisations and they were" also in favour of the 
change. The Law Commission, in its 110 th Report, the Christian Women's 
Commission, Members of Parliament a nd other community leaders have all 
been requesting us to make a change in  this provision.

just to bring the Indian Christians at  par with the words 'Mohammedans' used 
in section 213 so that they are also not expected to go through this

predecessor-in-interest. 
Since this is a provision which seeks to help the community and also 
delete one provision which is now considered unconscionable with regard to 
excluding a widow from her husband's property, I request the hon. House to 
take it up for consideration and pass it.

SHRI S. NIRAIKULATHAN (Tamil Nadu): Sir, I rise to speak on the 
National Commission for Safai Karamcharis Amendment Bill, 2001, on behalf 
of AIADMK. 
This Bill seeks to extend the te rm of the present Commission up to 
29,h February, 2004. The National Commission for Safai Karamcharis was 
originally set up in 1994. Even after 8 years, the conditions of safai 
karamcharis have not improved. 
The National Human Rights Commission and the National 
Commission for Safai Karamcharis had decided to eliminate manual 
scavenging several years before. But this practice is still going on. 
Employment of Manual Scavengers and  Construction of Dry Latrines 
(Prohibition) Act was passed in 1993. Yet, it was not implemented 
wholeheartedly. Under the Constitution, every citizen has a right to live with 
dignity.   But these safai karamcharis live in misery and squalor because they 
307 

RAJYA SABHA [3 December, 2 001] 
all belong to the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. The so-called 
'vamasrama' is being practised, so far as safai karamcharis. I am sorry to say 
this.   But this is a fact. 
I say so because, in 1992, the Centre launched a scheme known as 
National Scheme of Liberation and Rehabilitation of scavengers and their 
dependents. The aim was to abolish manual scavenging and provide alternate 
employment to the scavengers and their dependents. Today, after almost 10 
years, we are once again speaking about abolishing this inhuman practice. If 
there is any single leader in this count ry who cares for the welfare of the 
SC/STs, it is my respected leader and former Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu, Dr. 
Puratchi Thalaivi. When my leader became the Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu in 
1991, she launched a scheme to rehabili tate the safai karmacharis. Under the 
scheme, the Tamil Nadu Adi Dravida De velopment Corporation gave loans to 
safai karamcharis for buying autos, taxi cars and mini lorries. Even tanker 
lorries were provided on loan basis to groups of karamcharis. 
Not only this, scholarships were given to SC/ST students for pursuing 
studies. My leader knew that the SC/ST people could get social and economic 
freedom only through education. That is why, my revered leader provided free 
bicycles to girl-students of 11 th and I2 m class. The AIADMK Government 
withdrew even the anti-SC/ST rule brought by the DMK Government and 
which was a hurdle in the way of prom otion of SC/ST employees of Tamil 
Nadu. 
So, my request to the hon. Minister is, please formulate a scheme 
whereby sufficient funds could be made available to them. He should see to it 
that all the class IV workers in the country live with dignity. 
With these words, I conclude.

BILL, 2001 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (SHRI 
MUNI LALL):   Sir, I move: 
"That  the  Bill  to  repeal the Tea  Districts  Emigrant  Labour 
(Repeal) Act, 1970,   be taken into consideration." 
The Commission on Review of Administrative Laws, under the 
chairmanship of Shri P.C. Jain, has recommended repeal of the Tea Districts 
Emigrant Labour (Repeal) Act, 1970. 
The Tea Districts Emigrant Labour (Repeal) Act, 1970 repealed the 
Tea Districts Emigrant Labour Act, 1932. However, the Tea Districts Emigrant 
Labour (Repeal) Act, 1970 retained the ri ght of repatriation provided under 
section 12 of the Tea Districts Emig rant Labour Act, 1932 subject to the 
following conditions, namely: 
(I) if on commencement of the Tea Districts Emigrant Labour 
(Repeal) Act, 1970, a three year period of stay of an emigrant 
labourer, who entered Assam after the 3 rd August, i960 had 
expired, he was given a period  of six months from the 
commencement of the Act to exercise the right of repatriation, 
or 
(II) if three years' period of st ay of an emigrant labourer who 
entered Assam before the commencement of the Act of 1970 
expired after the commencement of the said Act, then he 
could exercise the right of repat riation within six months of 
the expiry of such period of three years. 
As the period mentioned in parag raph 2 above has expired, the Tea 
Districts Emigrant Labour (Repeal) Act, 1970 is no longer required. The Bill, 
accordingly, seeks to repeal the Tea Districts Emigrant Labour (Repeal) Act, 
1970. I request this august House to consider and pass the Bill. 
The question was proposed.

The Cine-workers Welfare Fund (Amendment) Bill, 2001 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (SHRI 
MUNI LALL): Sir, I move: 
"That the Bill further to amend the Cine-workers Welfare 
Fund Act, 1981, as passed by the Lok Sabha, be taken into 
consideration." 
As the hon. Members are aware,  the Cine-workers Welfare Fund 
Act,'1981 is a piece of progressive social welfare legislation enacted for the 
benefit of cine - workers. The Act envi sages extension of welfare measures 
such as health, medical care and educational assistance to cine - workers and 
their family members. The corpus of t he Fund is created out of a Cess levied 
and collected as a duty of excise on feature films certified by the Central 
Board of Film Certification, which is credited to the Consolidated Fund of India 
under Section 5 of the Cine-workers Welfare Cess Act, 1981. 
The fund is utilised for financing activities to promote the welfare of 
workers employed in cine industry. Presently, there are approximately 63,000 
cine-workers in the country, out of wh ich only 30,000 workers are getting 
benefits under the ongoing welfare sc hemes. The reason is that the 
wage/remuneration limit prescribed un der the Act has become insignificant 
and a large Viumber of workers remain outside the scope of definition Of cine-
workers due to increase in their wages/remuneration over a period of time. 
The ceiling of Rs.1,600/- p.m., where remuneration is paid by way of 
monthly wages, or a sum of Rs.8,000/- where such remuneration has been by 
way of lump sum, is prescribed under sub-section (b) (ii) of Section 2 for 
making the cine-workers entitled to welfare benefits under the Act. 
321 

RAJYA SABHA [3 December, 2001] 
This ceiling was last revised in 1987 by  an amendment of the Act. Since then 
there has been substantial increase in the wages/remuneration of cine-
workers. But since there has also b een a commensurate increase in prices, 
there has been a continuous demand to  increase the wage/remuneration limit 
under the Act so that the cine work ers, who are presently outside the 
definition of cine-workers due to incr eased wages/remuneration, are also 
covered under the definition of cine-workers for the purpose of the Act. 
In view of the aforesaid facts and in  order to bring the bulk of the 
hitherto uncovered cine-workers under the ambit of the welfare provisions, it is 
proposed to remove the existing ceiling on wages/remuneration given in 
Section 2 (b) (ii) of the Cine-work ers Welfare Fund Act, 1981, and authorise 
the Central Government to prescribe t he wages/remuneration of cine-workers 
by issue of notification in the Gazette of India fr om time to time, by an 
amendment to Section 2 (b) (ii) of the Cine-Workers Welfare Fund Act, 1981, 
so that increase in the ceiling of remuner ation of cine-workers, in case it is 
considered necessary and desirable, can be notified from time to time without 
amending the Act frequently. 
By this amendment, more cine-workers would be added thus raising 
the total number of cine-workers to be covered under the welfare provisions. 
With these words, I commend the Bill for the unanimous support of 
the august House. 
The Question was proposed.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Report of the S.L. Kapoor Committee on Credit to SSI 
*201. SHRI CR THIR UNAVUKKARASU: Will the Minister of 
FINANCE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Committee on Credit to Small Scale Sector under the 
chairmanship of Shri S.L. Kapur has submitted its report to Government; 
(b) if so, the details of the main recommendations; 
(c) whether Government have examined the report; 
(d) if so, action proposed to be taken by Government thereon; and 
(e) the other measures proposed to be taken by which S.S.I, funds reach 
the grassroot level? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) to (e) A Statement is laid on the Table of the 
House. 
Statement 
Reserve Bank of India (RBI) had in December, 1997 appointed a One 
Man Committee headed by Shri S.L. Kapur, the then Member, Board for 
Industrial & Financial Reconstruction (BIFR) to review inter-alia (i) the working 
of credit delivery system of small scale industries with a view to making the 
system more effective, simple and effi cient to administer and (ii) to make 
suggestions for simplification and improvements in systems and procedures. 
The Committee submitted its report to RBI on 30th June, 1998 which contains 
126 recommendations. Out of 126 recommendations, 103 have been examined by 
the RBI and decision taken thereon. Banks/Financial Institutions and other 

RAJYA SABHA [4 December, 2001 ] 
agencies have already implemented 86 recommendations. Some of the important 
measures taken pursuant to the recommendations of the Committee include: 
(0  De-linking of SIDBI from IDBI. 
(ii)  Opening of more specialized Branches. 
(iii) Enhancement in the limits of Composite Loan from Rs. 2 lakhs to Rs. 
5 lakhs. 
(iv)   Setting up of more DRTs. 
(v)  Introduction of Credit Guarantee Scheme. 
(vi) Raising the exemption limit for collateral security from Rs. 25,000 to 
Rs. 5 lakhs. 
Seventeen Recommendations have not been found feasible for acceptable 
at this stage. However, review of policies and procedures is a continuous exercise. 
Remaining 23 recommendations are under examination at various stages. Other 
measures taken by Government and RBI for promotion and development of 
Small Scale Industry inter-alia include the following: 
(i) RBI advised banks to follow the procedure of sanctioning working 
capital limits computed on the basis of minimum of 20% of the 
projected annual turnover to all SSI Units requiring aggregate fund 
based working capital limits upto Rs. 5 crores 
(ii) RBI Advised banks to ensure that out of their total fundsient to SSI 
Sector, at least 40% should be made available to units with investment 
in Plant & Machinery upto Rs. 5 lakhs and 20% should be made 
available to units with investment in plant and machinery between 
Rs. 5 lakhs and Rs. 25 lakhs. 
(iii) Increased the Project Cost Limit under National Equity Fund (NEF) 
Scheme from Rs. 10 lakh to Rs. 25 lakh (Union Budget 2000-2001) 
and further to Rs. 50 lakh. Like-wise Soft Loan component on NEF 
has also been raised to Rs. 10 lakhs. 
(iv) RBI advised Banks to fix sub-limits within overall limit to the large 
borrowers specifically for meeting the payment obligations in respect 
of purchases from SSI. 
2 

[4 December, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
(v) Introduced Credit Linked Capital Subsidy for the upgradation of the 
Small Scale Industries. 
(vi) Enhanced limits of Composite Loan to Rs. 25 lakhs, and raised 
exemption limit for collateral security to Rs. 5 lakhs.

† *202 SHRI JANESHWAR MISHRA: Will the Minister of PETROLEUM 
AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that abundant sources of oil/gas have been found in

(c) whether it is also a fact that Government are considering to entrust the

(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI RAM 
NAIK): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (d) Commercial reserves of hydrocarbons have not yet been 
established in the State of Uttar Pradesh. 
However, in order to accelerate pace of exploration efforts in the country. 
Government approved in February, 1997, a New Exploration Licensing Policy 
(NELP) providing a number of attractive fiscal and contractual terms to the 
bidders, from both public and private sectors, to participate in the activities of 
exploration of hydrocarbons. Under this Policy, companies have the freedom 
to market the oil and gas produced fr om the contract area in the domestic 
market. Blocks GV-ONN-97/1 and GV-ONN-2000/1 in the State of Uttar Pradesh 
covering areas of 36,750 sq. km. and 23,500 sq. km. respectively were awarded 
to the consortium of Oil & Natural Gas Corporation Ltd. and Indian Oil 
Corporation Ltd. (ONGC-IOC) under the first round and second round of NELP 
respectively.

SHRI YASHWANT SINHA: Sir, it is nobody's case and certainly not

taken. The Government is aware of the fact that there is slowdown in the 
Indian economy. I have already explained about the slowdown in the Indian 
economy. I had stood in this House and explained that there were some 
external reasons for the slowdown. The external reason, as I had mentioned 
in this House on a previous occasion,  is the collapse of the technology 
stocks in the USA which impacted on our technology sector also. It is because 
of the increase in the international oil prices which went up by almost 300 
per cent starting from 1999 and throughout 2000—until the prices softened 
recently that we had to raise the co nsumer price of petroleum products 
which had an impact on the growth of consumption. In fact, the consumption, 
except in the month of October when it had picked up, has gone down. 
Diesel consumption has actually declined. So, these are the global factors.

slowdown phase, I have repeatedly said, is the slowdown in the Indian 
agriculture over the last two years, i.e. 1999-2000 when the contribution of

of our people live in rural areas and depend on agriculture and allied sectors,

States share in small savings 
*207. SHRI S. NIRAIKULATHAN : Will the Minister of FINANCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Reddy Commission has recommended that 
the entire amount collected from a State under small savings be given to that 
State itself instead of giving only 80 per cent of the collection; 
(b) if so, whether the recommendation has been accepted; and 
(c) by when it is likely to be implemented? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI YASHWANT SINHA): (a) The 
Expert Committee on administered interest rates and other related issues, set up 
under the chairmanship of Dr. Y. V. Reddy, Deputy Governor of Reserve Bank of 
India has, inter-alia, recommended arrang ements, for transfer of entire net 
proceeds under small savings schemes to the concerned State Governments. 
(b) and (c) The Committee has also suggested "a wider debate on various 
issues involving all stakeholders and wider consultation (particularly with the 
States) in respect of the Committee's recommendations regarding small savings". 
The report has, accordingly, been placed on the official website of the Ministry 
of Finance to invite response from the public and the State Governments. The 
Committee's Report will provide an input into Government's approach on this 
subject.

Fall in ground-water level in Andhra Pradesh 
*210 DR. DASARI NARAYANA RAO: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a)whether it is a fact that the ground-water level in districts of Srikakulam 
and Chittoor of Andhra Pradesh has, gone down the level of more than four 
metres thereby making the situation alarming; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c)the remedial measures Government propose to take in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) to (c) Yes, 
Sir. Ground water levels in certain parts of the districts of Srikakulam and 
Chittoor in Andhra Pradesh have declined by more than four metres. 
Decline in levels of ground water in certain parts of Srikakulam district 
last 10 years has been from 0.01 to 5.72 metres in pre-monsoon periods 
whereas in chittoor district, it has been from 0.27 to 4.39 metres in post-
monsoon periods. 
Water being a State subject, it is primarily the responsibility of the 
concerned State Government to plan, finance and execute schemes 
for augmenting water resources. Government of India is also promoting 
rainwater harvesting through Watershed Management Programme, artificial 
recharge of ground water and roof top rain water harvesting under various 
schemes. Various measures as initiated by the Central Government for water 
conservation and augmenting ground water resources are indicated 
below:—  
 (i)   Constitution of Central Ground Water Authority under the 
Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 for regulation and control 
of ground water management and development. 
                               (ii)       Circulation of a Model Bill to all the States / Union Territories to 
27 

RAJYA SABHA [4 December, 2001 ] 
enable them to enact suitable legislation for regulation and control 
of ground water development. 
(iii) Circulation of Manual on artificial recharge of ground water to the 
States / Union Territories to enable them to formulate area specific 
artificial recharge schemes to check the declining trend in ground 
water levels. 
(iv) Implementation of Pilot Central Sector Scheme on "Studies on 
Artificial Recharge of Ground Water" in the country at an estimated 
cost of Rs. 25.00 crore. Recharging wells and rain water harvesting 
are integral part of this scheme. The results of the scheme have been 
found to be very encouraging. 
Under-Utilization of Kochi Airport 
*211. SHRI R.P. GOEKNA: Will the Minister of CIVIL AVIATION be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether the huge infrastructural facilities and flight handling 
capacities created at a cost of Rs. 309 crores at the newly build private 
international airport at Kochi continue to be grossly underutilized causing 
heavy losses for the last three years; 
(b) if so, the extent of losses suffered with reasons therefor; 
(c) whether it is a fact that although a number of international carriers 
have expressed interest to operative from Kochi, their requests are being 
ignored to avoid competition for the national carriers, thereby sending wrong 
signals to other prospective investors; and 
(d) the details thereof and action taken thereon? 
THE MINISTER OF CIVIL AVIATION (SHRI SYED SHAHNAWAZ 
HUSSAIN): (a) and (b) The ineternational airport at Cochin belongs to the 
State Government of Kerala and is a joint venture with the private sector. It 
is one of the two international airports in Kerala besides Thiruvananthapuram. 
International flights of Air India and Indian Airlines also operate out of Calicut. 
Therefore the infrastructural facilities etc. built at the Cochin airport was with the 
full knowledge of the parties concerned about operations of international 
flights from other airports in Kerala. The Government of India does not 
have any information in respect of losses suffered by the Cochin airport. 
The same is being obtained from State Government / Cochin International 
Airport Limited (CIAL). 
28 

[4 December, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) Providing international connectivity  from different airports is a 
matter of the Central Government and is decided during bilateral air services 
consultations at Government level based on reciprocity. The competing demands 
from other States are also kept in mind. 
(d) Cochin lias been granted as a point of call to Oman Air and Silk Air 
(Singapore). Apart from this Emirates Airline of Dubai has also been granted 
access to Cochin effective September, 2002. Therefore it will be incorrect to say 
that Cochin is being ignored while considering demands of foreign airlines for 
additional points of call. The requests of other airlines such as Yemen Airways, 
Qatar Airways, Saudia, Gulf Air, Sri Lankan Airlines, Uzbekistan Airways will be 
discussed during bilateral discussions with their respective Governments as 
and when held.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) and (c) State Bank of India (SBI) has reported 
that it had participated in a global bid floated by Commercial Bank of Ethiopia 
(CBE) for management contract of CBE and SBI's bid was accepted. SBI has

gross non-performing assets to gross advances of the SCBs had improved from

increased by 7.9% during the year ended 31st March, 2001. Thus, the Indian 
Banking Industry is not on the verge of failure in domestic field. 
Changes in Credit Policy 
*217. DR. KARAN SINGH: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether the Reserve Bank of India has lately announced drastic 
changes in the credit policy for Banks, reducing the bench mark Bank-rates 
to a 28 years low of 6.5 per cent and slashing the Cash Reserve Ratio from 
7.5 per cent to 5.5. per cent; 
(b) the reasons warranting such changes in the credit policy; 
(c) whether it affects the already poor incentives for the common 
depositors, the workers, the aged and the pensioners to deposit their savings 
in banks; and 
(d) how far the new credit policy is pro-corporate and anti-common 
depositors, the workers, the aged and the pensioners? 
42 

[4 December, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE 
(SHRI BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) On a review of macroeconomic and 
monetary developments, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) reduced Bank Rate 
by 0.5 percentage point from 7.0 per cent to 6.50 per cent with effect from the 
close of business on October 22,2001 as a part of monetary policy measures 
which are announced six monthly. At this level, it is the lowest Bank Rate since 
May 1973. Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) was also reduced by 200 basis points to 
5.50 per cent from 7.50 per cent of Net Demand and Time Liabilities 
(NDTL).  
(b) All scheduled commercial banks (excluding regional Rural Banks) 
were required to maintain with the RBI a CRR of 7.5 per cent of their NDTL 
prior to announcement of the mid-term review. While the statutory minimum 
requirement of CRR maintenance at 3.0 per cent is obligatory on the banks 
additional CRR, ranging between 4.5 per cent and 12.0 per cent since 1981, 
was imposed from time to time in order to reduce the overflow of liquidity 
due to excessive money supply in the economy. With a view to rationalizing 
CRR prescription and moving towards the long term goal of keeping CRR 
normally at the statutory level, changes were made in respect of the coverage 
as well as the level of CRR for the banking system. 
It is expected that the recent changes in policy with regard to CRR 
will facilitate the development of a short term yield curve, develop money 
market, reduce the regulatory arbitrage between banks and non-banks, 
enhance the availability of lendable resources with the banks and improve 
the efficiency of indirect instruments in the conduct of monetary policy. 
(c) and (d) The commercial banks are free to determine their interest 
rate structure on bank deposits excepting savings bank accounts, keeping in 
view their own asset liability structure. In addition, banks are permitted to 
formulate fixed deposit schemes specifically meant for senior citizens offering 
higher and fixed rates of interest as compared to normal deposits of any 
size. 
The changes in interest rates are in consonance with the decline in 
inflation and as such are not expected to affect the interest of common 
depositors adversely. .

RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) to (c) Water 
being a State subject, the responsibility of survey and investigation, 
planning, development funding, execution and management of all types of 
water resources projects including flood control and drainage to harness 
the water resources within the States rests with the concerned State 
Government according to their own priorities and from their own plan 
resources. The National Water Policy inter-alia envisages augmenting 
the availability of water by adopting measures for maximizing retention and 
minimizing losses, recharging ground water, a dopting water harvesting 
practices, making water available to water short areas by inter-basin 
transfer based on a national perspective and recycling and re-use of 
water. 
India receives a rainfall of about 4000 Billion Cubic Metre (BCM) 
including snowfall every year. As per the latest assessment made by the 
Central Water Commission, the average annual flow in the river systems of 
India is about 1869 BCM. However, due to topographical and environmental 
constraints, natural evaporation and vegetation losses the utilisable surface 
water resources by conventional methods has been assessed as 690 BCM. 
For storage of rain water, about 3600 large dams and reservoirs and 250 
barrages have been constructed in the country. Through these dams, a total 
live storage capacity of 177 BCM has been created upto 1995. An additional 
live storage capacity of 75 BCM will be created on completion of the dams, 
which are under various stages of construction. Proposals to take up additional 
dams to create a live storage capacity of 132 BCM are also under formulation/ 
consideration. The live storage capacity and the percentage of storage capacity 
being stored at present in each State is given in the statement, (see below) 
Besides, about 2,53,000 Tanks (minor dams) and ponds have also been created 
in the country. The replenishable ground water resources are of the order of 
432 BCM out of which about 154 BCM has been developed for use. 
Government of India is also promoting rainwater harvesting through 
Watershed Management Programme, artificial recharge of ground water 
and roof-top rainwater harvesting unde r the sector reform project of 
Accelerated Rural Water Supply Programme under the Ministry of Rural 
Development, for which technical and Financial assistance is provided 
to the State Government and other implementing agencies. Central Ground 
Water Board has also taken up pilot studi es for artificial ground water 
recharge.

Change in security arrangements 
1511. SHRI C.P. THIRUNAVUKKARASU: Will the Minister of CIVIL 
AVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether any change has been introduced in the security arrangements at the 
National and International Airports after the attack on the World Trade Centre in 
USA; and 
(b) if so, the details of improvements made in the security arrangements? 
THE MINISTER OF CIVIL AVIATION (SHRI SYED SHAHNAWAZ 
HUSSAIN): (a) and (b) After the recent terrorist attacks in USA, the following security 
measures have been taken, inter alia, to further strengthen security at the airports in India 
in order to prevent hijackings and other unlawful interference with civil aviation 
operations:— 
(i)   Deployment of Central Industrial Security Force (CISF) at all 
operational airports in a time bound manner; 
(ii)   Deployment of Sky Marshals on all routes of scheduled domestic 
airlines, including private airlines; 
(iii)   Deployment of Quick Reaction Teams at major airports; 
(iv)   Strict access control, including mandatory ladder point security 
checks of passengers and their hand baggage; 
(v)   Security audit of airports, followed by necessary action for further 
strengthening of security arrangements.

1544. SHRIK. RAMA MOHAN RAO: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) to (c) Yes, Sir. The Mid-term Review of the 
Monetary and Credit Policy for the year 2001-2002 released by the Reserve Bank of 
India on October 22,2001 has placed its projection of growth of Gross Domestic 
Product (GDP) for the current year to a range of 5.0 per cent to 6.0 per cent for 
the Indian economy as against a projected GDP growth of 6.0 per cent to 6.5 
per cent for 2001-02 announced in its Annual Statement on Monetary and Credit 
Policy released on April 19, 2001. the GDP growth forecast 6.0 per cent to 6.5 
per cent for 2001-02 in RBI's Annual Statement was men based on the reasonable 
monsoon, good performance of exports and a revival of the industrial sector beginning 
second quarter of the year. The scaling down by the RBI of the GDP growth 
projection in its Mid-term Review of the Monetary and Credit Policy takes into acount 
positive developments regarding the likely rate of growth in agriculture during the 
current year on the one hand the unfavourable behaviour of industrial and export sectors 
and assumes that there would be no further disruption in the world economic 
environment.

104 

[4December,2001] RAJYA SABHA

Growth rate of the economy 
†1598. SHRI BALKAVI BAIRAGI: Will the Minister of FINANCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that now India is not among one of the two 
fastest developing economies; 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
122 

[4 December, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) whether it is also a tact that as per the report of the IMF the growth rate is 
likely to fall by 4.5— 5 per cent; 
(c) whether according to the report the growth rate of India is very low as 
compared to the required rate to remove the poverty; and 
(d) if so, the details of the effective measures taken to spur the falling growth 
rate on the track along with the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) to (c) As per the World Economic Outlook (WEO) 
October 2001, published by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) the real growth in 
India's Gross Domestic Product (GDF) is projected at 4.5 per cent for 2001 or 5 per 
cent for the financial year 2001-02. These October 2001 WEO projections were made 
before the September 11 terrorist attacks. In view of those events, and more recent 
data suggesting that the global economic situation before the attacks was weaker than 
earlier projected, the IMF has revised down its baseline projections for global 
growth. Given that India is less exposed to global developments the growth in 
calendar year 2001 in India is now projected by the IMF to be 4.4 per cent (or 
4.7% in fiscal year 2001-02). Under the revised projections released by the IMF on 
November 13,2001, India is one of the three fastest growing large economies in the 
world, the other two are China and Russia which are expected to grow by 7.3 per 
cent and 5.8 per cent respectively in 2001. It may be noted that Reserve Bank of 
India in its Mid Term Review of Monetary and Credit Policy has placed its 
projection of GDP growth for 2001-02 in the range of 5.0 per cent to 6.0 per cent for 
the Indian economy, the WEO October, 2001 notes that aGDP growth rate of 4.5 per 
cent in India is well below levels considered necessary to make significant inroads 
into poverty. However, WEO does acknowledge that over the last three decades, 
India's poverty rate has declined significantly. 
(d) The Budget for 2001-2002 has provided enhanced central plan outlays for 
key infrastructure sectors and increased emphasis has been placed on accelerating 
capital investment expenditure. Besides, Reserve Bank of India on the basis of a 
review of macro-economic and monetary developments took certain monetary 
measures keeping in view need for adequate liquidity to meet credit growth and 
support revival of investment demand consistent with price stability. These 
measures included further reduction in the bank 
123 

RAJYA SABHA [4 December, 2001] 
rate from 7 per cent to 6.5 per cent, rationalization and reduction in the Cash 
Reserve Ratio for the banking system and reduction in the maximum interest rate 
chargeable on export credit by 1.0 percentage point for a period of six months 
with effect from September 26,2001. These specific measures to stimulate 
demand in the backdrop of budget strategy are expected to have a favourable 
impact on growth.

Parliament by law to be expedient in the public interest is in the Union List. 
However, water, that is to say, water supplies, irrigation and canals, drainage and 
embankments, water storage and water power subject to the provisions of Entry 56 
of List-I is with the State Governments as per Entry 17—State list. There is no 
proposal with the Government to change any of these provisions in the 
Constitution. 
(b) Does not arise. 
Reclamation of Lands Swallowed by Rivers 
1663. SHRIMATI AMBIKA SONI: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the plight of people in parts of Uttar 
Pradesh who have been rendered homeless and landless due to the change in the 
course of Yamuna rivers; 
(b) if so, what steps Government have taken in this regard; 
(c) whether other areas with similar problem have been identified; and 
(d) whether Government expect a pan-Indian effort towards reclamation of 
land swallowed by rivers which have changed their course? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) to (d) As per information furnished by the Government of Uttar 
Pradesh, they have taken up basin wise approach to contain the course of 
183 

RAJYA SABHA [4 December, 2001] 
river Yamuna. In first phase, 27 flood protection scheme have been taken up and 
completed in the Yamuna basin by them to check the change in the river course. 
Further, change of course by rivers being a natural phenomenon known as 
meandering of rivers, it is neither possible nor viable to check the same in whole 
length of rivers. However, in selected reaches, where it is necessary to protect 
the important structures, townships, etc. suitable flood protection measures are 
taken up. 
Statutory Powers to River Board Organisations 
1664. DR. ALLADI P. RAJKUMAR: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Statutory powers for River Board Organisations in the 
management of water resources have been opposed by certain State 
Governments; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) what is Government's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) to (c) National 
Water Resources Council (NWRC) while deliberating the draft revised National 
Water Policy in its 4th Meeting held on 7th July, 2000 considered inter alia the 
provision relating to setting up of River Basin Organisations (RBOs) with 
statutory powers. Some of the States like Goa, Himachal Pradesh Kerala, Madhya 
Pradesh, Maharashtra, Punjab and Uttar Pradesh had opposed the setting up of 
RBOs with statutory powers. In view of the divergent views expressed on this 
provision relating to RBOs and other provisions of the draft revised National 
Water policy by the members of NWRC, a Working Group under the 
chairmanship of Union Minister of Water Resources was constituted to 
examine the draft provisions. The Working Group has discussed this issue and 
after arriving at a near consensus, it has recommended to NWRC inter-alia a 
draft provision on setting up of RBOs without proposing the 
statutory/regulatory powers thereto.

Proposal to raise water level of Mullapperiyar Dam 
SHRI N.K. PREMACHANDRAN (Kerela): Sir, it is very reliably 
learnt that there is a strong move to raise the water level of 
Mullapperiyar Dam in Kerala from 136 feet, without considering the 
genuine reservation of the Government of Kerala. The proposal to 
raise the water level of the Dam will adversely affect the environment. 
The increase of water level tends to destroy the forest and wild life of 
the surroundings, especially the Tiger  Reserve Project of Periyar in 
Kerala. 
The Mullapperiyar Dam was constructed long back and the 
strength and capacity of the Dam is in doubt. The safety of the Dam is 
in danger. During the recent continuous monsoon, high leakage of 
water was found through the Dam, causing apprehension among the 
people. 
If anything happens to the Dam, the population of Idukki, 
Kottayam and Ernakulam District will be totally affected and they will 
be devastated. All-party Conference convened by the Chief Minister of 
Kerala has already appealed to the Go vernment of India not to raise 
the water level of Mullapperiyar Dam. 
Considering all these facts, it is urged that the water level of 
Mullapperiyar Dam shall not be raised at any cost. 
SHRI A. VIJAYA RAGHAVAN (Kerala): Sir, I associate myself 
with what the hon. Member has said.

Depletion of grassland at Kaziranga Wildlife Sanctuary 
SHRIMATI BASANTI SARMA (Assam): Sir, through this 
Special Mention, I would like to mention about the Kaziranga National 
Park, which is being attacked by a destroyer plant called 'Maimoja'. 
This plant, which is of 'the touch-me-not plant variety', has covered 
more than 200 acres of land in the National Park. All these are 
grassland areas and an attraction to the herbivorous animals found 
here. As a result of this, food has become scarce to the wildlife 
endemic in this area. The creeper-like plant, which is growing in almost 
all the ranges in the Park, is destroying the grassland and also climbs 
to a height of 10-12 feet. Kaziranga is the habitat of the world-famous 
one-horned rhinoceros. As the plant called 'Maimoja' is attacking the 
grassland, the officials concerned are worried about the situation, as it 
might destroy the grassland of the area. Last year, an attempt was 
made to uproot and destroy the plant, with the help of tractors, but it 
failed. This plant was never seen in this area before. It is believed that 
the seed of this 
220 

[4 December, 2001] RAJYA SABHA  
plant has taken root due to erosion during yearly floods when most of 
the area in the Kaziranga Park remains submerged. So, through you, 
Sir, I urge upon the concerned Ministry to look into the matter and 
take immediate measures to contain this menace; otherwise, the 
future of this world-famous Park looks very bleak and it will have a 
disastrous effect on the animals found here. Another point that I 
would like to mention here is we sh ould stop the illegal plundering of 
vines which grows in abundance here; otherwise, it will hamper the 
growth of our cane industry. Thank you, Sir.
