last revised in 1987, has a ceiling of Rs. 1,600 per month or Rs.8,000 
per film 
234 

[4 December, 2001]      RAJYA SABHA 
and there has been such a substantial increase in the wages of cine-
workers in keeping with the price rise, really no significant number of 
cine-workers have been able to access  this fund. Therefore, this was 
a long standing demand coming from t he film industry to raise this 
ceiling. Therefore, I welcome it. I say this because the film industry 
owes, in a large measure, its existence to the workers who have been 
working for long hours at great risk to their life and health for the film 
industry, but they never get reco gnised when it comes to the film 
winning laurels or awards or in making profits. If I am recognised 
today as an actress, it is not only in a large measure due to the 
producers, writers and direct ors, who have given me these 
opportunities, but also due to the cine-workers working in various 
disciplines and in various collaborations to make the effort possible. 
Therefore, I welcome the Bill. 
Sir, the question, however, is what happens to these funds 
once they are collected. It has bee n brought to our notice that though 
during the last many years Rs.20 crores have been collected in these 
funds, they have not been given to  the workers only because the 
ceiling before this was very low. Out of this, the administrative cost of 
looking after this fund was about Rs.6  crores to Rs.8 crores. So, we 
were wasting a very valuable fund that was lying with us. 
What is the mechanism for the producers or the workers 
associations to recommend a case and say that this worker needs 
access to these funds? There have been horror stories of workers 
dying in the throes of illness. When they fall ill, they apply for financial 
assistance from this fund. But it is a long, arduous, way of going 
through the Government machinery to get access to this fund. The 
worker never benefits from it. Therefore, we need to simplify the 
procedure so that the affected pers ons can have easy access to this 
fund. It can be a simple letter from the Association saying that this 
worker legitimately deserves financial help from this fund. If the worker 
is ill, an immediate instalment should be released. Then, another 
instalment should be released, rather than saying, "First, you pay the 
money and only after that will we give you the money," It is not 
possible for the people who do not have the money. 
235 

RAJYA SABHA [4 December, 2001]  
There has been a long standing demand from the All India 
Film Employees Confederation for increasing the subsistence 
allowance which I completely endorse. In view of the steep rise in the 
prices -- the present rates were fixed long back -- the subsistence 
allowance, under the scheme, for the treatment of heart diseases, 
kidney transplantation, cancer, etc ., should be increased; otherwise, 
they cannot avail of as sistance from this fund. This is not sufficient, 
under the present requirements. They have to succumb to the illness. 
In the case of the beedi and mine workers, the Labour 
Welfare Organisation has taken the initiative of implementing the 
integrated housing scheme. The same scheme should be extended to 
the cine workers so that they can ava il of this facility. The Ministry of 
Labour is administering various welf are funds for workers in the beedi 
industry, cine industry, mining industry, limestone industry and 
dolomite industry, etc. Most of these schemes in the area of health, 
education, housing, recreation and water supply are common. 
Therefore, it would be appropriate to have a uniform scale of benefits 
with regard to the financial assistance and other norms for all such 
common schemes under the welfare fund. 
Now, the television industry  has expanded exponentially. 
This industry is providing employ ment to thousands of technicians, 
craftsmen. If the same technicians are working in advertising, short 
and documentary films, no cess is collected from the television 
industry or from the advertising i ndustry or from the film industry. 
Nothing is available to the workers working in this industry. Since 
convergence is taking place in all the media, this fund should not 
deprive these workers. The television channels are making payment to 
television software producers. Our suggestion is that they can deduct 
a certain amount per episode as cess. The amount can be decided or 
it can be fixed. So, the television industry also should be included in 
this. How are these funds dispersed? Now, there is a Commissioner's 
Office at Nagpur. Earlier they used to have representatives from the 
people within the film industry. But this is no longer necessary. Now, 
we suggest that on that body, y ou have people representing all the 
regional languages so that they can have an idea of what is going on 
there. Then, audited acco unts must also be given to these 21 craft 
unions that these are the funds ava ilable and this is the amount which 
can be made available, because information is really what is required 
at this moment. People even do not know of these schemes and the 
audited accounts. There   should   be   accountability,    and   total   
transparency   should   be 
236 

[4 December, 2001]     RAJYA SABHA 
maintained. This should be made possible. People from the film 
industry should be represented on the Board,  as we used to have in 
the past. 
Now, there is one thing that film-makers of very low-budget 
films have been saying, and that ca n be given some consideration. 
That is, Rs. 20,000 per film, which t he rest of the producers are very 
happy to give. It has started with Rs. 2000, then, Rs. 10,000 and then 
it became Rs.20,000; and the producers have been giving this money 
very happily. But we have films which are made on a huge budget; we 
have films which are made on a shoe-string-budget, particularly, a lot 
of regional language films, a lot of what is called parallel cinema films 
are made on shoe-string-budgets. For the producers of shoe-string-
budget films, it becomes a constriction to pay even this Rs. 20,000. 
So, they say that it is not fair to have a blanket amount as the money 
to be paid by the producers. They are making films on a budget that 
goes up to Rs. 20 crores. At the same time, a film is being made even 
in less than Rs. I crore. So, a suggestion which is being mooted is 
those films which are made under a budget of less than a crore can 
be asked to pay only Rs. 10,000. I re quest the Minister to give due 
consideration to this point. And those films which exceed a budget of 
Rs. One crore, could pay Rs. 20,000 which, I think, is a valid demand 
and we would also be helping the regional cinema and independent 
film-makers that do not have the funds. 
Having said this. I welcome the Bill.

SHRIMATI VANGA GEETHA (Andhra Pradesh): Mr. Vice-
Chairman, Sir, I thank you for giving me this opportunity to speak on 
this Bill. I support the Cine-worke rs Welfare Fund (Amendment) Bill, 
2001. I am happy that the Government has considered those workers, 
whose monthly wages or lump sum remuneration has increased over 
a period of time, and has magnanimously increased the monthly 
wages limit from Rs. 1,600/- to Rs. 8,000/- and a lump sum 
remuneration limit from Rs. 8,000/- to Rs. one lakh. This is definitely a 
welcome sign, and I am sure that the cine workers and the films 
fraternity will be grateful for the steps taken by the Government. 
It is good that the Government has brought forward this Bill. I 
welcome this measure, but while supporting this Bill, I want to point out 
certain problems of the cine worker s, who are a worried lot. The very 
important part of this Bill is the r egistration of workers. Who are going 
to be registered under this Welfare Fund? This Act is for the welfare of 
the people in the industry. The phra se 'Five feature Films' has been 
mentioned as a condition to get the benefit of this Act. There is no 
producer who has finished five feature films. Within one film itself, the 
producer goes out of the industry. Therefore, an amendment would not 
help in the present situation. The wage and remuneration limit 
prescribed under the Act has become insignificant due to increase in it 
over a period of time. The industrial workers who are in the cine field 
are now included in this Act. Under the Act, any worker has to register 
himself according to the agreement. Only then, he would become a 
worker and could get the benefits from the Cine-Workers Welfare Fund 
Act. There is the Cine-Workers Welfare Cess Act, 1981. The Cess Act

crores of rupees are invested in the production of a film. The fund 
should be increased. The registration of  a worker in itself is a very big 
task for an ordinary person. To go inside an association is a very big 
problem.    I would suggest that the Government

[4 December, 2001] RAJYA SABHA  
should  consider that  aspect.     There should  be  a comprehensive  
Bill, covering the provisions of the three Acts so that all are benefited 
by it. 
The Bill has to protect almost all the sections in the film 
industry. Everybody know s that the small screen industry is really 
becoming very large and the cinema industry is decimating. So, this 
Amendment Bill is very necessary. 
Further, I would like to talk about the disparity in the fees. The 
persons behind the camera are not given enough remuneration. They 
are, in a way, being exploited. This must be taken care of in this Bill. 
This Bill does not cove r the exhibition side.  Nowadays, everybody 
wants to close the cinema halls and put up a shopping complex or 
build a marriage hall or residential houses there. But what will happen 
to those workers who have been working there for the last 30 or 40 
years? This part also needs to be covered. 
The film industry is, totally, under a slump, dominated by 
mega serials. The workers, the actors and the artistes are not 
migrating to TV serials. Is a cess levied on TV serials? Or, is some 
money collected from them? They are making money in many ways, 
by putting advertisements in-between the serials. The Government 
should also take this aspect into consideration. At the same time, the 
interests of the artistes who are in this field should also be protected 
by the enactment of this Bill as they  are facing a lot of competition. I 
feel that this amendment is appreciated only in one way, for including 
the word instalment" which is not found in any other Act. This word is 
very useful because the workers are pa id in instalments. This type of 
development and this type of focus should be there. A more 
comprehensive Bill should be brought to protect the workers and the 
industry in all manners. 
Sir, I feel that not only the workers but also the artistes should 
be included in it. This Bill shoul d be more comprehensive. The 
theatres also should be included in an amended form. The Jatra 
artistes who play a very significant role should also be included. The 
figure Is much more than what is stated in the Bill, and it is not 
60,000. The number of the workers an d the staff working in serials 
and mega serials is much more. Their interests should be taken care 
of. The cine-workers should be provided the trade union rights.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN  THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR 
(SHRI MUNI LALL): Mr. Vice-Chairman,  Sir, I am very thankful to the 
hon. Members who have participated in the debate and have made 
very valuable suggestions. We are very much alive to the situation. 
The hon. Member, Shri Sangh Priya Gautam, has raised certain 
doubts about the fixation of ceiling which has not been mentioned in 
the Act. The fixation of ceiling of remuneration and wages will be done 
after taking several issues into consideration, i.e. the Price Index, 
decision of the Pay Commission and several other things. The amount 
will be fixed reasonably. There is no doubt about it. The hon. Member, 
Shri Virumbi, raised certain issues regarding the growth of industry. 
He has expressed his concern about the decline in the film industry. 
Many other hon. Members have also expressed their concern about it. 
Sir, the film industry is a fluctuat ing industry. It is a fabulous industry. 
There might be one or two stray cases. But a majority of the industry 
which is engaged in the production of films is in a fabulous condition. 
The Cess which has been fixed at Rs. 20,000 and Rs. 10,000 is not 
much. Many hon. Members have suggested that it should be raised. 
But it is a reasonable amount. We have taken a balanced view of it. 
We will see how it can be disbursed properly. Some hon. Members 
raised certain points regarding t he distribution system.   The 
distribution system is 
241 

RAJYA SABHA [4 December, 2001]  
perfect. The Welfare Commission is taking into account all these 
things. Some hon. Members stated that too much expenditure has 
been incurred on the administrative se t-up. I am happy to inform-the 
august House that not much expenditure has been incurred on the 
administrative set-up because one Commission is looking after many 
items. So far as the expenditure incurred on the administrative set up 
is concerned, it is negligible. Shrimati Shabana Azmi has suggested 
some valuable improvements. Shrimati Saroj Dubey has expressed 
concern about disbursement, ac cident benefits and some other 
benefits. There is a Group Insurance Scheme which is applicable to 
the cine-workers also. The Group In surance Scheme covers the cine-
workers. The Labour Department and many other Departments are

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CHEMICALS 
AND FERTILISERS (SHRI SATYA BRATA MOOKHERJEE):   Sir, I 
move: 
"That the Bill further to amend the National Institute of 
Pharmaceutical Education and Research Act, 1988, 
be taken into consideration." 
Sir, the Act was passed in 1988. The idea was to take over 
the management and assets and liabili ties of what is popularly known 
as NIPER. In the NIPER, there is a Board of Governors, and Section 4 
(3) (o) provides for nomination of Members - two Members from the 
Lok Sabha and one Member from t he Rajya Sabha - by the Speaker 
of the Lok Sabha and by the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. Now, sub-
section (4) of Section (4) provides for the tenure of office of other 
Governors, which is a fixed tenure of three years. But, so far as 
Members of the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha are concerned, there 
is no tenure fixed. So, this amendment seeks to introduce a proviso to 
sub-section (4), under which the tenure will be fixed in the event of a 
Member of the Lok Sabha or of the Rajya Sabha becoming a Minister 
or a Minister of State or a Deputy Minister or the Deputy Chairman of 
the Rajya Sabha; in which case, he automatically ceases to be a 
member of the Board of Governors.  That is the proviso which is 
sought to be introduced. This Bill is merely for removing the anomaly 
and providing specifically for the t enure of office of members of the 
Board. 
The question was proposed.

situation. In such a situation, t he issue is not concerned with labour, 
but it is the policy question which is  called for. Therefore, even in the

Statement 
(a) The country is endowed with an economically viable hydro potential 
assessed at 148700 MW in terms of installed capacity. However, only 16.6% of 
this potential has been harnessed, 6.3% is under various stages of development 
and 2.73% has been cleared by the Central Electricity Authority (CEA). 
(b) Hydro power development has been constrained on account of technical 
problems, geological difficulties and surprises, inaccessibility of sites, delay in 
land acquisition, environmental considerations, resettlement of project affected 
families, and law and order problems in militant infested areas. 
(c) and (d) Government of India is according high priority for development 
of hydro-electric projects in the countr y and has so far tentatively identified 
hydro-electric projects of 16,291 MW for benefits in the Xth Plan and 22,364 
MW for benefits in the Xlth Plan. The capacity addition identified for benefits 
in these Plans would however depend on obtaining statutory clearances, project 
initiatives and tying-up of necessary funds. 
In order to accelerate the process of survey and investigation of the new 
hydro-electric sites and to create a shelf of feasible projects which could be 
taken up for execution, the CEA has brought out a Report on Preliminary Ranking 
Study of about 400 hydro schemes with an aggregate installed capacity of about 
1,07,000 MW which were identified but are yet to be developed. This study 
would enable potential hydro developers to take up detailed survey and 
investigation, cost estimates and tentative tariff for the most attractive and viable 
schemes in each basin in a phased manner. The Government is exploring various 
possibilities of funding and executing hydro-electric projects after extensive 
consultations with the States, financial institutions and entrepreneurs. An 
International Conference on non-fossil fuel Generation has been scheduled in 
February, 2002.

SHRI SURESH PRABHU: Sir, the power generation from a hydroelectric station 
depends on the availability of water. If the reservoir level goes down, obviously, it is 
going to affect the generation in hydroelectric station. Last year, as per the India 
Meteorological Department, the rainfall was 92 per cent of the normal average. In fact, 
the water-storage system, from which we actually generate power, was operating at 
the below average level. As a result of that, because of low rainfall, many of our 
hydroelectric generation targets have been affected very adversely. It has not happened 
in India only. For example, in Brazil, they generate more than 92 per cent of power 
from hydro resource. They had to resort to 30 per cent power cut because of less 
availability of water. So, the availability of water determines to what extent we can 
generate power from a hydro-electric power station. Therefore, the low utilization of 
capacity, as far as hydro-electiic power stations are concerned, is attributable directly to 
the low rainfall and low reservoir level during the last year. Hopefully, the situation 
will improve. In fact, it has gone down in Andhra Pradesh. This was one of the reasons 
why Andhra Pradesh was facing such a problem. Andhra Pradesh did not receive 
enough rains. Even Karnataka did not receive enough rains. As a result of that, it had 
gone down there also. Therefore, this is the only criterion, that is, availability of water, 
on which the utilization will depend. Of course, it depends on demand also. But, in this 
case, it is not attributable to demand. It is directly attributable to low availability of 
water.

Procedure for promotion of Army Officers 
1694. SHRIMATI AMBIKA SONI: W ill the Minister of DEFENCE be 
pleased to state: 
67 

RAJYA SABHA [5 December, 2001] 
(a) the procedures and parameters adopted for promotion of Army Officers; 
(b) whether it is a fact that several ex cellent officers who played admirable 
role in Kargil have been left out and some officers named in Tehelka have 
been promoted; 
(c) if so, the reasons for the same; and 
(d) what steps are being taken to correct this undesirable situation? 
THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI GEORGE FERNANDES) (a) to (c) 
Promotion of officers in the Army is to two categories i.e. the category of 
Non-Select ranks Captain, Major and Lieutenant Colonel (Time Scale) and the 
category of Select ranks i.e. Lieutenant Colonel (by selection), vCo!onel, 
Brigadier, Major General and Lieutenant General. 
Promotion to Non-Select ranks is on the basis of time stipulation provided 
the mandatory qualitative requirements are satisfied. 
The procedure for promotion of Army Officers to select ranks is governed 
by Paragraph 108 of the Regulations of the Army under which the Chief of 
Army Staff (COAS) is empowered to convene Selection Boards. Promotion to 
select ranks is by a system of screening by independent Selection Boards 
constituted from select officers based on their operational and staff experiences, 
based on inputs available from records of an officer. Suitability for promotion 
is based upon value judgement of members of Selection Boards on the basis of 
data examined from the overall reckonab le records of past performance and 
potential of the officer. Selection made is based on vacancies available and on 
comparative merit. Selection Board proceedings for the rank of Lieutenant 
Colonel and Colonel are approved by the COAS under delegated powers. Similar 
proceedings for promotion to ranks of Brigadier, Major General and Lieutenant 
General are approved at the level of Government. 
Fairness in Selection Boards is ensured by not disclosing the identity of the 
officer under consideration for promotion upto the rank of Brigadier. Different 
officers are incorporated as observers to witness the Board proceedings so as to 
bring about transparency and objectivity. No officer named in Tehelka episode 
has so far been promoted. 
(d) Selection procedures in the Army are time tested and proven over the 
years.

Fake currency notes supplied to militants 
† 1720. SHRIMATI SAVITA SHARDA:  Will the Minister of HOME 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that fake currency notes are supplied by the Kashmiris 
to the terrorists hiding in Delhi and other parts of the country; 
(b) if so, whether Government have taken any steps to curb such activities, 
so far; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI I. D. SWAMI): (a) Available info rmation indicates that Indian fake 
currency notes are being clandestinely inducted into the country from across 
the Indo-Pak Border, Indo-Nepal Border and the Bangladesh-Myanmar Border. 
This is being done through smugglers, pilgrims and terrorists and insurgent 
groups. During the last three years viz. 1999 to 2001 (up to 15.11.2001) 40 
cases of circulation of fake currency have been registered in J&K. 
(b) and (c) 'Police' and 'Public Orde r' are State subjects as per the 
Constitution of India. As such registration, investigation, detection and 
prevention of crime is primarily the responsibility of the State Governments. It 
is for the State Governments to devise various methods and take concrete steps 
to counter such activities. 
The Union Government have taken the following steps to curb this 
menace:— 
(i) The Central Bureau of Investig ation has created a special unit for 
exclusive investigation of counterfeit currency notes. The Border 
Security Force has alerted its forward troops to be more vigilant so as 
to ensure that such currency notes are not smuggled into the country. 
(ii) A High Level Committee has been  constituted with representatives 
from the Department of Economic Affairs, Reserve Bank of India, 
Ministry of Home Affairs/ Nationa l Security Council Secretariat, to 
go into the entire gamut of issues pertaining to the circulation of fake 
Indian currency. 
(iii) A six-member Fact Finding Committee was set up under the 
convenorship of Shri V.K. Gaikward, Dy. General Manager, RBI, 
comprising experts on note-printing/ currency paper etc. for examining 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
83 

RAJYA SABHA [5 December, 2001 ] 
the fake notes seized in the past in order to enable the Government to 
take remedial action vis-a-vis printing and security features. The 
Committee has submitted its report. 
(iv)   RBI has been advised to go in for a publicity campaign about security 
features incorporated in the genuine notes. 
The Reserve Bank of India has taken the following steps: 
(1) The security features of Rs. 500 denomination notes has been widely 
publicized in the print media to help the people detect fake notes. 
(2) A film on security features of Rs. 500 denomination notes produced 
in English, Hindi and other regional languages has been telecast on 
Doordarshan. 
(3) For the benefit of public, a booklet has been brought out which inter-
alia, describes the features of genuine notes. This booklet has been 
placed on the RBI website besides be ing available to the public for 
sale at RBI's issue offices. 
(4) RBI has also offered to impart tr aining to officials in the State 
Governments in the detection of fake currency notes. 
The Ministry of External Affairs have been taken up the matter with 
Government of Nepal. Both the sides have expressed determination to take 
urgent necessary steps to prevent the misuse of Nepalese territory for activities 
directed against India. 
Instructions are also issued to all State Governments, from time to time to 
take appropriate measures for curbing the menace of circulation of fake currency

Tackling extremist forces in North East 
1750. SHRI DRUPAD BORGOHAIN: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS 
be pleased to state: 
(a) what latest strategies Government have adopted to fight the menace 
perpetrated by extremist forces of North East Region like ULFA, BLT, NDF 
(B), NSCN (IM), NSCN (K), TNV, etc.; 
(b) whether Government are planning to have peace talks with these 
organisations; and 
(c) if not, whether Government are making plans to strike at the terrorist 
organisations with some harsh laws and to use structures like unified command? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI l.D. SWAMI): (a) to (c) The Government has taken various steps to 
fight against the militancy in the North Eastern States. These include, inter-
alia, deployment of para-military forces and army in the States, coordinated 
action by army, para-military forces and State Police for counter militancy 
operations, declaration of major militant groups as unlawful associations under 
the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967; declaration of militancy affected 
States as disturbed area under the Arme d Forces (Special powers) Act, 1958; 
reimbursement of security related expenditure to the State Governments and 
modernization/upgradation of State Police Force. Regular review of the situation 
both at State and Central Government level is being made. 
The Government has extended an invitation to all those who have strayed 
from the paths of togetherness to come forward for talks within the four corners 
of our Constitution. Union Government have entered into ceasefire agreements 
with National Socialist Council of Nagaland (I/M faction) [NSCN (I/M)] on 
25th July, 1997 and with Khaplang faction [NSCN(K)] on 28th April, 2001. In 
Assam, the Bodo Liberation Tiger (BLT ) has come forward for peace talks 
abjuring the path of violence. Kuki National Army (KNA) of Manipur has 
offered for negotiation with Government. Other militant outfits have not 
responded for talks within the parameters indicated.

Installation of solar geyser in the State Government buildings 
†1763. SHRI RAJNATH SINGH 'SURYA': Will the Minister of NON-
CONVENTIONAL ENERGY SOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have requested to all the State Governments for 
installation of solar geyser on their buildings; 
(b) the names of States which have shown their interest in implementing these 
schemes and the States which have not shown their interest in the same; and 
(c) the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF  THE MINISTRY OF NON-
CONVENTIONAL ENERGY SOURCES (SHRI M. KANNAPPAN): (a) Yes, Sir. 
The Ministry of Non-Conventional Energy Sources have requested all the 
State/Union Territory Governments in 1993 to issue suitable directives for 
installation of solar water heating systems in Government hospitals and hotels and 
also for other categories of buildings like guest houses, laboratories, hostels, 
police/army barracks, canteens, industrial establishments etc. where need for hot 
water exists. In April, 1994, the Ministry of Urban Development (MUD) 
requested the State Government to consider issuing suitable directives to the local 
bodies under their control for modifying the building bye-laws with a view to 
make the installation of solar water heating systems mandatory in hotels and 
hospitals in commercial sector. In order to assist the local bodies to amend their 
building bye-laws for making use of solar water heaters mandatory, a model 
regulation/bye-laws has also been drafted and has been circulated by MUD in 
April, 1999. The model regulation, when adopted by the local bodies, will make 
it mandatory for several categories of building including residential buildings of 
certain minimum plinth area, to have solar water heating systems. 
(b.) So far, the Government of Andhra Pradesh, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, 
Madhya Pradesh, Punjab, Rajasthan and the Union Territory of Dadra and Nagar Haveli 
have issued instructions to their concerned establishments in this regard. Further, the 
Government of Rajasthan has circulated the Model Rajasthan (Municipal area 
building), ReguIation-2000, with mandatory provision for solar water heating systems 
in certain categories of buildings with die directives that these are to be implemented 
by the concerned Municipal Development Trust/

Municipal Corporation/Municipal Councils/Municipalities of the State. The rest of the 
States/UTs have not taken any such decision so far. The Ministry has been

State/UT Governments include lack of awareness of the benefit of using solar 
water heaters, high initial cost and hot water not being required for most part of the 
year.

Proposal of waiving a percentage of interest surcharge owed by 
SEBs 
1771. SHRI SOLIPETA RAMACHANDRA REDDY: Will the Minister of 
POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government propose to waive a percentage of interest surcharge 
owed by different State Electricity Boards; 
(b) if so, the names of three top benefi ciary State Electricity Boards, who 
stand to benefit by Centre's above gesture; and 
138 

[5 December, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) whether Andhra Pradesh State Electricity Board will get benefit from 
this; if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRIMATI 
JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) A Conference of Chief Ministers/Power Ministers 
held in March 2001 under the Chairman ship of the Prime Minister resolved 
that an Expert Group would be set up to recommend a one time settlement of all 
Power Sector past dues to Central Public Sector Undertakings (CPSUs) and 
dues from CPSUs to State Power Utilities. The Expert Group was set up under 
the Chairmanship of Shri Montek Singh Ahluwalia. The Group proposed a 
scheme of settlement of outstanding dues linked to a mechanism that would 
ensure payment of current dues in future. The recommendations of the Group, 
inter-alia, included securitisation of the outstanding dues through bonds issued 
by the respective State Governments. The recommendations included waiver 
of 50% of surcharge/interest accrue d on outstandings. The High Level 
Empowered Group of Chief Ministers who accepted the recommendations of 
the Expert Group has suggested an increase in the waiver from 50% to 60%. 
(b) The scheme would be available to those states which agree to sign a 
tripartite agreement with the Central Government and the Reserve Bank of India. 
As such, it is premature to list the top beneficiaries at this stage. 
(c) Andhra Pradesh State Electricity Board had outstanding dues of Rs. 1178 
crores to CPSUs of Ministry of Power, Department of Coal, Atomic energy and 
Ministry of Railways as on 28.2.2001. This included a surcharge of around 
Rs.544.49 crores. On implementation of the scheme for one time settlement of 
dues 60% of this surcharge would be waived. 
Spectrum Power Project in Andhra Pradesh 
1772: SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA: W ill the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that an investigation into the Spectrum Power Project 
in Andhra Pradesh shows the extent of corruption, institutional rot and 
administrative collapse that has corroded the system and highlights the bizarre 
risks of doing business in India; 
(b) several public sector banks led by SBI and seven institutions led by IDBI 
are under threat of ending up with large bad debts on their books; and 
(c) if so, what action Government is taking on this issue? 
139 

RAJYA SABHA [5 December, 2001] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRIMATI 
JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) The 208 MW Godavari power project being 
implemented by M/s. Spectrum Power Generation Limited (SPGL), was awarded 
for implementation through private sector by the State Government of Andhra 
Pradesh and the Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) in respect of the project has 
been signed between the erstwhile Andhra Pradesh State Electricity Board and 
SPGL. The Central Government has received some representations alleging 
misappropriation of funds and other irregularities by SPGL, which have been 
forwarded to the State Government. The various allegations made against SPGL 
are presently subjudice in various Courts in the country as well as the Supreme 
Court and the Central Government (Ministry of Power) has not so far carried 
out any separate investigation into the matter. 
(b) The AP Transco have informed that they have been making monthly 
payments promptly to SPGL and no default of payment by SPGL has been 
intimated to them by any bank. However, the IDBI has informed, that upon 
completion of the project, the Company was burdened with skewed debt equity 
ratio which, as on 31.3.1999 was 5.22:1 (against an envisaged debt equity ratio 
of 2.33:1) leading to a debt liability th at cannot be serviced with the present 
level of tariffs received by the Compan y from AP Transco. IDBI have further 
informed that SPGL was in default to the institutions for an aggregate amount 
of Rs. 1440 million as on 30th June, 2001. The main reason cited by the Company 
for experiencing the liquidity constraints resulting in non- payment of dues to 
the Financial Institutions are (i) reimbursement of tariffs based on the original 
project cost aproved by CEA (Rs.7.48 billion) and not on the revised project 
cost (Rs.9.90 billion) which has impacted the cash flow of the Company; (ii) 
inability of the Company to raise equity capital (Rs. 1.15 billion) due to embargo 
by the Court, due to litigation between promoters; and (iii) non-availability of 
regular working capital facilities from banks, etc. According to IDBI,-the 
Company has been indicating that it is exploring possible alternatives for raising 
long term funds to clear the dues of the Financial Institutions. Pursuant to recent 
Supreme Court order, the Company has pl anned to raise preference capital to 
be mainly used for repayment of dues of institutions, which will also rectify the 
skewed debt equity structure. 
(c) The various representations received by the Central Government (Ministry 
of Power) have been referred to the Government of Andhra Pradesh, who have 
not so far conveyed their views in the matter. The issues involved are subjudice, 
in various Courts. The Central Electricity Authority (CEA) has issued a 
140 
 

[5 December, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
provisional Techno-economic Clearance to the Godavari project and the final 
completion cost of the project as well as the corresponding financial package 
will be examined by CEA for approval after all the relevant details are submitted 
to them by the Government of Andhra Pradesh/Transmission Corporation of 
Andhra Pradesh Limited (AP- Transco).

National Programme for rejuvenating traditional water resources 
1794. SHRI SATISH PR ADHAN: Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Rural Development Ministry decided to begin a National 
Programme to rejuvenate traditional water resources; 
'(b) if so, details thereof; 
(c) the steps Government have so far taken or propose to take to revive water 
resources; 
(d) whether Union Government is seriously considering to bring any legislation 
to regulate the use of ground water in view of over-exploitation in the country; and 
(e) if so, details thereof and when it will be implemented? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI ANNASAHEB M.K. PATIL): (a) to (c) Rejuvenation, including 
desilation of traditional water resources like village ponds / tanks, is proposed to be 
taken up as one-time exercise under the Watershed Development Programmes and other 
Schemes being implemented by the Ministry of Rural Development. 
(d) and (e) A Model Bill to regulate use of ground water was circulated to the 
States in 1970 by Ministry of Water Resources for making necessary legislation. 
Later, the Bill was revised and circulated to the States again in 1992. The Bill was again 
revised and circulated to the States in June 1996. The State Government of Gujarat 
has enacted legislation. Tamil Nadu has passed Metropolitan Area Ground Water 
Regulation Act. The State Governments of Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Andhra 
Pradesh have passed regulation for drinking water purposes. West Bengal and 
Karnataka have also passed Bills for water resources conservation, protection and 
development.

Plight of Virginia Tobacco Growers in Karnataka 
SHRI H. K. JAVARE GOWDA (Karnataka): Sir, about 50,000 farmers 
of Karnataka State grow Virginia Tobacco and produce about 50 million kgs. of 
high quality Virginia tobacco, bulk of which is exported. The rest is used for 
cigarettes and other tobacco-related products. 
About five lakh farm workers are dependent on Virginia Tobacco 
cultivation. For constructing tobacco barns and raising crops, the farmers have 
taken loans to the extent of about Rs.600 crores from various financial 
institutions. Tobacco is a monsoon crop an d it is drought-resis tant since it is 
being grown in drought-prone areas only.  The farmers have no alternative but 
to continue growing Virginia Tobacco for their survival and existence.    The 
prices had dropped steeply over the last two years in 
198 

[5 December, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
Karnataka. The price has reduced from Rs.55/- to Rs.37 per kg. Smuggling of 
premium international brand cigarettes, which amounts to 10% of the 
production of the country, is affecting the Indian farmers severely and causing 
loss to the exchequer. High excise duty and 15% surcharge has resulted in 
the decline of domestic demand and a fall in prices. 
The Virginia Tobacco growers are facing hardship as they are not 
getting remunerative prices for tobacco and they are not able to pay back their 
loans. They are left with no option except  to stop the cultivat ion. I, therefore, 
urge upon the Government to check the smuggling of cigarettes, reduce 
excise and surcharge duties, provide incentives for export by providing 
remunerative prices and help the tobacco growing farmers of the State.

Surplus Stock of Sugar in Uttar Pradesh and Maharashtra 
SHRI BACHANI LEKHRAJ (Gujarat): Sir, there is a problem of plenty 
in sugar production in Uttar Pradesh and Maharashtra. There are no takers for 
this surplus stock of 30 lakh metric tonnes in U.P alone. Stocks are expected 
to increase further in the current crushing season. In U.P., the net sugar 
production is expected to touch a new high of ever 47 lakh metric tonnes. In 
Maharashtra, sugar production will be more than this. This surplus stock of 
sugar has already been reflected in the market. The price of sugar in the open 
market has come down, in spite of t he festive season. On the other hand, 
prices of cane have been increased by Rs .25 a quintal. As a result of this, the 
cost of sugar has gone up. This excess production, with no outlet for export, 
has put the sugar industry under strain. The future of the sugar industry seems 
to be bleak. The ex-factory price of a 100 kilogram sugar bag has come down 
from Rs. 1,4.15/- in the year 2000, to Rs. 1,380/- and further to Rs. 1,320/- in 
the year 2001. The mills have suffered a net loss of Rs.250 crores on levy 
sugar meant for the public distributi on system. Hence, the Government is 
requested to allow the sugar mills to release their surplus stocks in the open 
market and also to arrange for export of sugar; otherwise, it will adversely 
affect the sugar mills and sugarcane producers.

PUBLIC GRIEVANCES AND PENSIONS, MINISTRY OF PLANNING, 
DEPARTMENT OF ATOMIC ENERGY AND DEPARTMENT OF SPACE 
(SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA RAJE):   Sir, I move: 
" That the Bill further to amend the Constitution of India, as passed 
by the Lok Sabha, be taken into consideration." 
Mr. Chairman, Sir, on 26 th November, 2001, I had introduced the 
Constitution (Ninety-second) Amendment Bill. 2001, in the Lok Sabha. This 
was to amend the article 16 (4A) of t he Constitution retrospectively, that is, 
from 17 th June, 1995. It would provide for consequential seniority to the 
Government servants belonging to the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled 
Tribes in the case of promotion by virtue  of the rule of reservation with a view 
to negate the effects of the Departm ent of Personnel and Training Office 
Memorandum dated 30.1.1997. The Bill was passed by the Lok Sabha on 28th 
November, 2001. 
It may be recalled that the O.M. dated 30.1.1997 was issued to give 
effect to the so-called catch-up principle', this was laid down by the Supreme 
Court in the case of Virpal Singh Chauhan and in the case of Ajit Singh-l. This 
was subsequently reiterated by the C onstitution Bench in the case of Ajit 
Singh-ll. The issue of O.M. dated 30 .1.1997 had adversely affected the 
seniority of the Government servants belonging to SC/ST category promoted 
before General/OBC candidates on ac count of reservation policy. The 
Government had reviewed the position in the light of views received from 
various quarters and in the interest of the SC/ST Government servants, it was 
then decided to bring forth a Constitu tion amendment to negate the effects of 
O.M. dated 30.1.1997 immediately. Just a withdrawal of the O.M. of 30.1.1997 
would not meet the desired purpose, as  the law laid down by the Supreme 
Court would otherwise prevail. So, the amendment to article 16(4A) of the 
Constitution to provide for the consequential seniority also in the case of 
promotion by virtue of rule of rese rvation has been introduced. It is also 
necessary to give retrospective effect to the proposed Constitutional 
amendment to article 16(4A) with effect from the date of coming into force of 
article 16(4A) itself, that is, from the 17th June, 1995.

I may also mention here that the National Commission for Scheduled 
Castes and Scheduled Tribes was also consulted in this regard and the 
Commission has appreciated our move to carry out such an amendment. 
After the Constitution (Ninety-second) Amendment Bill, 2001, 
becomes an Act, Government would be empowered to grant consequential 
seniority also to the SC/ST Government servants on their promotion by virtue 
of rule of reservation. 
Sir, with these words, I commend this Bill to the House. 
The question was proposed.

this particular Amendment Bill is meant to get over certain difficulties, as the

her statement in this House. And the hon.  Minister has rightly said that merely 
the withdrawal of the Circular of 30 th January, 1997 would not have been

context, the hon. Minister has referred to two Judgments in the Statement of 
Objects & Reasons, namely, the Judgmen t in the case of Virpal Singh

statement before the House, the hon. Minister has now referred to Ajit Singh 
No. II. So, what is this Constitutional amendment trying to achieve? From time 
to time, as you know, in matters of recr uitment and promotion, there is a roster 
system in terms of which promotions  were granted to the members of 
Scheduled Castes/Scheduled Tribes on th e basis of a quota which is fixed. 
The roster is set on the basis of that quota. What happened in Chauhan's case 
was that despite the fact that the quota was filled and the promotion was 
given, there was a circular of the Railways which said that even though 
promotions were given to the me mbers of the Scheduled Castes and 
Scheduled Tribes, they would not get th eir seniority within the quota. The 
Supreme Court said that under arti cle 16(4), which has been part of the 
Constitution, it was permissible for the Government to give them accelerated 
promotion, without giving them seniorit y. That was the decision in Chauhan's 
case. I compliment the hon. Minister fo r seeking to undo that decision through 
a Constitutional amendment, namely, now it will not depend on a circular by

SHRI K.B. KRISHNA MURTHY (Kar nataka): At the outset, Madam, I 
would like to express my gratitude to you for giving me an opportunity to 
speak on this Bill. Mr. Cho. Ramaswamy opposed this Bill. I would like to say 
that out of the 32 crores Scheduled Caste population, only 40 lakhs are 
employed in the Government, and my friend here said that this amendment is 
going to destroy the future of many youths in this country. Madam, I beg to 
differ with him. 
I - possibly there may be many - am disturbed at the gradual erosion 
of the basic legislative intent of rese rvation envisaged by the founding fathers 
of our Constitution, by a stream of Apex Court Judgements, due to vague 
interpretations of Articles 16(4), 46 and 335. .In recent times, due to the. 
interpretations of the Supreme Court, the Constitutional guarantees under 
Articles 16(4), 46 and 335 have been diluted. A plain interpretation of Articles 
16(4), 46 and 335 is as follows: 
While Article 16(4) provides for reservation of appointments under 
the State for members of the Scheduled Castes by way of an exception to the 
guarantees under Article 16(1), Article 46 is a directive to the State to promote 
the economic interests of the Schedu led Castes and Scheduled Tribes; and 
the first part of Article 335 enjoins upon the State to take into consideration 
the claims of members of the Schedu led Castes and Scheduled Tribes in 
making appointments under the Government. Madam, while complying with 
this direction under Article 335, the provisions of Articles 16(1) & 46 should be 
read together. Going by this interpre tation, it follows that the special 
consideration under Article 335 will exte nd to initial recruitment as well as 
promotions to higher posts under the Government. 
229 
 

RAJYA SABHA [5 December, 2001] 
Inspite of the clarity provided in Articles 16(4), 46 and 335, the 
Supreme Court is applying vague legal dynamics and delivering judgements, 
which, by letter and spirit, oppose the legislative intent of these sacred 
Constitutional guarantees to the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. 
The Supreme Court judgements are conflicting with the Constitutional 
provisions relating to reservation policy governing promotions. There seems to 
be diverse opinions in judgements, whic h have conflicted with each other in 
the cases relating to promotion for the Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe 
Government employees. 
Madam, some demotions have taken place in Karnataka also. Many 
engineers have been humiliated. In the Badappanavar case, a cruel joke was 
played on the Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe engineers. They were 
initially recruited on reservation basis as Junior Engineers, and some rose to 
the position of Superintending Engineer s and Chief Engineers. The Supreme 
Court, in this case, allowed seniority to these Engineers up to the level of 
Executive Engineers and declared the seni ority from there onwards, at par 
with the general category. This judgment was given retrospective effect and in 
the consequence many Superintending Engineers were demoted as Executive 
Engineers and Chief Engineers as Superin tending Engineers. Great injustice 
was caused to these Engineers, who we re humiliated. Taking the above facts 
into consideration, the Government shou ld enact suitable laws and bring them 
within the orbit of the 9th Schedule to prevent interference from the courts. 
Regarding vacancy-based roster to post-based roster, an Office 
Memorandum has been issued, it has to  be withdrawn. As per the Supreme 
Court judgment, all backlog vacancies should be filled up before Implementing 
the post-based roster system. Hence I appeal that this OM may be withdrawn. 
I request the hon. Minister to give directions to all state Governments 
to reinstate the officers who have been demoted to their original postings 
where they were before their demotions. 
The Government should come out wi th a clear picture of what is 
going to happen to the Scheduled Caste/Scheduled Tribe employees, who are 
working in the public sector undertakings.    Now as the public sector

THE CONSTITUTION (NINETY-SECOND AMENDMENT) BILL, 2001 - 
Contd. 
SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA RAJE: Madam Deputy Chairman, I 
would like to thank all the hon. Member s who have participated in this debate, 
and reiterate, at the same time, the Government's sincerity and commitment to 
the cause of the welfare and uplift of  the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled 
Tribes. We have, over the last two years, discussed this issue threadbare. 
And, very recently, this was discussed again in the Lok Sabha. In the couse of 
the discussion on the Bill that was brought  by Shri Pravin Rashtra Pal in the 
Lok Sabha, the hon. Prime Minist er made a promise there, on 18 th March, 
1999, that the Government would review  the O.M.s issued by the Department 
of Personnel and Training. And, in line with this thinking, two Constitution 
amendments had been brought, and we intend to issue orders very quickly so 
as to start the special recruitment drive.  Today, we are bringing in the third 
Constitution Amendment through the 92 nd Constitution (Amendment) Bill. This 
has been passed by the Lok Sabha and, now, we have brought before this 
House. This deals with the O.M. dated 30th January, 1997, and this is the O.M. 
which caused considerable anxiety to the hon. Members. 
This OM lays down a catch-up principle which allows general 
candidates to regain seniority over reserved candidates who have been given 
these accelerated promotions. It was iss ued in pursuance of the judgment of 
the Supreme Court in Ajit Singh(i) and Virpal Singh Chauhan's case. The 
Government sought legal opinion and consulted a wide cross-section of 
Members. Despite the fact that the catch-up principl e has been reiterated by 
the Supreme Court in the Ajit Singh(2) case, the Government has decided to 
amend the Constitution to allow memb ers of the Scheduled Castes and the 
Scheduled Tribes to retain their seniority on accelerated promotions. The 
Members would agree that this would tr anslate into reality the Government's 
resolve to mitigate the hardships t hat have been caused to members of the 
weakest classes by the issuance of the OM in 1997. 
 
241

RAJYA SABHA [5 December, 2001]  
Consideration of the Bill has witnessed a stimulating debate and many 
hon. Members, 18 altogether, have participated and presented their very 
esteemed views. There are some points that I would just quickly like to run 
over. They have touched upon comprehensive legislation, why there is laxity in 
Implementation of reservation, the progr ess that they wanted to know of the 
increase in representation of SCs and STs in Group A and B, reservation in private 
sector and judiciary, percentage of reservation to be revised according to the 
population and the OMs dated 2nd July, 1997 and 13th August 1997.  I would just 
like to run quickly over two or three Issues. 
Shri Raju Parmar made an additional point about the reservation Act 
which was introduced in 1996. This was moved by, what was called, the 
Ministry of Welfare then, and the idea was dropped subsequently. As far as 
sending of copies of the OM -- this was brought up in the Lok Sabha also - issued 
in pursuance of the constitutional amendments to all the State Governments is 
concerned, yes, we normally do this. In any case, we will take, up the suggestion 
and follow it up. 
Shri A. Vijaya Raghavan also touched upon all of these subjects and 
mentioned about reservation after disinvestment. The Government is committed to 
protect the Interests of the workers, as mentioned by the Finance Minister In 
the 2000-2001 Budget Speech. This was also brought up by Shri 
Krishnamurty. 
Shri Ramaswamy basically emphasised primary education, 
reservation and said that seniority should come by service and not by conferment 
and, therefore, opposed the Bill. 
Shri Kapil Sibal used all his eloquence to bring about some interesting 
points. He said we have still not done anything to undo the full effects of Ajit Singh 
(1) case. The Supreme Court in the case of M. G. Bandaperwar Vs. Karnataka 
has held that article I6(4){a) cannot help reserve candidates. He said that basically 
the Government is coming up with tokenism. The Constitution Amendment has 
been moved after a great deal of consultation with the Law Ministry, Law Officers 
of the Government and the National Commission of SCs and STs. The sole 
intention is to satisfy the D0PT8 OM which is dated 30 th January, 1997 and the 
Supreme Court judgment In pursuance of which the OM was issued. The broader 
issue of article I6(4)(a) and.its constitutionality is a subject of a set of petitions which 
are before the Supreme Court and, hence, efforts will be made to expedite this.   
The Government has also got passed two constitutional amendments 
242 

[5 December, 2001] RAJYA SABHA  
earlier to satisfy the effects of t he two earlier OMs. These have not been 
challenged judicially. Our move to move the third amendment is certainly not 
tokenism and, as far as the Government  is concerned, we are fully confident 
that we can defend the present amendment If It is challenged. He also spoke 
about the empowerment of the SCs and the STs. This is an issue which had 
been there over the last fifty years and it is now that something has happened 
this year. But I am on a very, very limited point which is the reservation in 
promotions, and, therefore,  I would like, to remind the House here that all of 
the Supreme Court's judgments have been pronounced between 1992 and 
1998 and it is only after this Government came to power that effective steps to 
mitigate the hardships that are suffered by the SC and the ST employees have 
been initiated. In the future also, the Government is committed to take all the 
necessary action to promote the just  causes of the SCs and STs and, I 
believe, this thinking is shared across the House. With these words, Madam, I 
seek the support of the hon. Members and commend this Bill to this august 
House to pass it.

my turn in the debate since yesterday. I am called as the last speaker and not 
the least. I am thankful to you. 
The attendance in the House reflects the interest we have towards 
solving unemployment. This problem is explosive today in our country. Day by 
day, the unemployment problem is gr owing, and there are no checks or 
preventive measures. There is no progr amme or policy which can check this 
growing problem. It is spreading like cancer. As cancer grows without any 
checks, just like that, the unemployment problem is growing. Both the Houses 
of Parliament have discussed this matter so many times; yet, in

opinion, there is no use of such discussions. 
 The problem is growing ever sinc e the early 50's, when we started 
planned   economic  development.   But   the   last   5   decades   of  
Planned Economic development has resulted in the rich becoming richer 
and  the poor becoming poorer. 
 That is the economic situation of  the country after 50 years of our 
Independence.   During the last one decade a new phenomenon has come

National Sample Survey in 1993-94 in its 50th round of analysis and its latest

the reason for this? I would like to submit that the main reason for the 
uncontrolled growth of unemployment is the new liberalised economic policy 
which does not have a human face and which is not concerned about the

a multinational company or, say, a rich person of a corporate house, invests

employment opportunities. They do not address the cause of the people

this policy. As a result of this, t here is growth of unemployment in the 
educated youth. There is growth of unemployment even among the

situation. Now-a-days if  a person gets employment even for one day in a

SHRI N.K. PREMACHANDRAN: I will be concluding with one more 
point. I would like to suggest one more point. It is, the right to work should be 
there as a fundamental right. Now, the Constitution (Ninety-third Amendment) 
Bill, 2001, is going to be discussed in  this august House either tomorrow or 
the day-after-tomorrow or in the coming days. There is a specific provision — 
amendment of 51A -- in this Bill which deals with Fundamental Duties. It says 
that it is the bounden duty of the parents or guardians to send their children to 
school. If it is the duty of the parents or guardians, my question is, whether 
there is any guarantee for jobs? We are imposing a duty on the parents or 
guardians that they should send their children to school, that they should not 
send their children to work. If you are imposing a duty on the parents or 
guardians that they should send their children to school, the State should also 
ensure job opportunities to the new generation or the growing population. 
With these words, I once again sa y that the present unemployment 
cannot be discussed in isolation of  economic policy. The problem of 
unemployment, the problem of poverty, has to be discussed alongwith the 
economic policies being pursued by this Government. The present economic 
policies, which are being pursued by this Government, are totally against the 
interests of the people, especially the unemployed people of this country. 
Therefore, the Government has to come forward with a clear policy or 
proposal so as to meet the situation or address' the problems. 
With these words, I conclude.  Thank you.

Satellite Money Orders 
*241. SHRI C. P. THIRUNAVUKKARASU: WUl the Minister of 
COMMUNICATIONS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Department of Posts has achieved the expected traffic of 
Satellite Money Orders; 
(b) if not, the reasons therefor; and 
(c) what steps Government are taking to improve the traffic of Satellite 
Money Order transfer? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMUNICATIONS (SHRr PRAMOD 
MAHAJAN): (a) to (c) Sir, a statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
1 

RAJYA SABHA        [6 December, 2001] 
Statement 
The Government had approved setting up of 75 Very Small Aperture 
Terminal (VSAT) stations as a part of 8th Five Year plan for transmission of 
Money Orders through Satellite system for cutting down delay in transmission 
and reducing manual handling of Money Orders thereby the cost of operation. 
The process of installation of VSAT network started towards the middle of 
1995 and 77 VSAT stations in place of  75 were installed by the middle of 
financial year 1996-97. 
The technology adopted for the VSAT was Code Division Multiple Access 
(CDMA) based micro-earth station having a bandwidth of 1.2 KBPS installed 
at Sikandarabad in Bulandshahar, Uttar Pradesh. Seventy-seven VSAT 
installed were networked with 610 Extended Satellite Money Order (ESMO) 
stations. 
At the time of planning for the VSAT system during 1992-93, the system 
was expected to capture about 25% of the total traffic of about 9.8 crores 
Money Orders. While six circles have captured more than 25% of the traffic, 
others could not do that on account of limitation of the technology like low 
bandwidth of 1.2 KBPS and capacity problem of the Remote Area Business 
Management Network (RABMN). With the increase in the bandwidth and by 
increasing the network by adding more ESMOs to the system, the flow of 
traffic could be increased to about 11.5 per cent of the overall traffic of 12 
crores Money Orders handled by the Department during 2000-01. 
Simultaneously, the Department on the advice of an Expert group took 
steps to set up high speed VSAT system on Time Division Multiple Access 
(TDMA) with 64 KBPS bandwidth. It has already installed 135 such high 
speed VSATs and 15 are under user testing. These stations are networked 
through 1350 ESMO stations. To this 400 more ESMO stations will be added 
to increase the flow of traffic through satellite. The old 77 VSATs on Code 
Division Multiple 
2 

[6 December, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
Access (CDMA) technology are also netw orked to the high-speed system to 
enable the Money Order traffic to be transmitted through the system.

Statement 
Incentives for Software Sector 
1. Export Promotion Capital Goods scheme (EPCG) has been rationalised 
and extended uniformly to all sectors without any threshold limit on 
payment of 5% duty. 
2. Approvals for all foreign direct investment proposals relating to the 
Information Technology sector, with the exception of Business-to-
consumer (B2C) e-commerce are under the automatic route. 
3. Software Technology Parks (STP) Scheme is implemented under the 
aegis of the Ministry of Information Technology through a single 
window mechanism of the Inter-Ministerial Standing Committee 
(IMSC). 
4. Accelerated depreciation norms for co mputers and computer peripherals 
for units under Export Oriented schemes (EOU/ EPZ/STP/EHTP) have 
been enhanced. These shall stand de preciated to overall limit of 90% 
over a period of 3 years instead of around 5 years earlier. 
5. DTA access upto 50% of the FOB va lue of export is permitted for 
software units under EOU/STP schemes. 
6. In . the 2000-01 Budget, Customs duty on Computers and Peripherals 
had been reduced from 20% to 15% and continues to be same. The 
Customs duty on all storage devices, integrated circuits, 
microprocessors, data display tubes and deflection components of colour 
monitors also continues at 0%. In the 2001-02 Budget, Customs duty on 
Information Technology Agreement (ITA-1) items of WTO (IT and 
Telecom products) has been reduced from existing 20—25% to 15%. 
7. Information Technology Software is exempted from Customs and Excise 
Duty. 
8. EOU/EPZ/STP/EHTP units are exempt ed from payment of Income Tax 
on export profits, upto 2010, in terms of Section 10A and   10B  of the  
Income  Tax  Act.   On  site  development  of 
26 

[6 December, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
computer  software  and services will  also  be  eligible  for tax 
exemption. 
9. Definition of Computer Software, as  in Section 80 HHE of the Income 
Tax Act has been widened to include transmission of data. 
10. Benefit of Section 80 HHE is available to supporting software developers. 
11. Exemption of withholding tax on interest on External Commercial 
Borrowings (ECBs) has been extended to the IT sector. 
12. IT Enabled Services have been made eligible for Income Tax benefit 
under Sections 10A, 10B and 80HHE of the Income Tax Act. 
13. A National Venture Fund for Software and IT Industry (NFSIT) has 
been set up with a corpus of Rs. 100 crores, out of which MIT shall 
contribute Rs. 30 crores. 
14. Income by way of dividends or long-term capital gains of a Venture 
Capital Fund or Venture Capital company from investment made by way 
of equity shares in a Venture Capital Undertaking, which has been 
expanded to include the Software and IT sectors, will henceforth not be 
included in computing the total income. 
15. To give thrust to Venture Capital finance, SEBI has been made the 
single point nodal agency for registration and regulation of both 
domestic and overseas venture capital funds.

1811. PROF. M. SANKARALINGAM: Will the PRIME MINIS

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF ATOMIC

State Government agencies for setting up such facilities in the country.

Sankhya Vahini Project  
1823.   DR.   Y.   LAKSHMI   PRAS AD:   Will   the   Minister   of 
COMMUNICATIONS be pleased to state: 
(a) what is the progress of the Sankhy a Vahini Project to create a high 
speed internet backbone in the country; and 
(b) the progress of laying optical fibre in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
COMMUNICATIONS (SHRI TAPAN SIKDAR): (a) The Sankhya Vahini 
Project to create a high speed data network in the country in collaboration 
with IUNet, a subsidiary of Carnegie Mellon University, USA has been 
shelved. 
(b) Does not arise in case of Sankhya Vahini Project. However, BSNL has 
plans to lay 1.26 lakh of OF Cable during this financial year & increase the 
Bandwidth in the country through Sanchar Sagar Phase-I & Phase-II & 
DWDM Projects. Sanchar Sagar Phase-I is having a Bandwidth (B/W) of 2.5 
Gbs & is working in 33 Major Cities. Sa nchar Sagar Phase-II is going to be 
completed in this financial year which will provide 2.5 Gbs BW to 185 
additional cities. DWDM Project will give a BW of 40 Gbs to all Major Cities 
of the country by 2003.

Competitors in International Long Distance Telephony Sector 
1828. SHRI SURESH PACHOURI: Will the Minister of 
COMMUNICATIONS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have considered the recent recommendations of the 
Telecom Regulatory Authority of India not to limit the number of 
competitors in the International Long Distance telephony sector; and

taken/proposed to be taken thereon? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
COMMUNICATIONS (SHRI TAPAN SIKDAR): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The recommendations. of Telecom Regulatory Authority of India 
(TRAI) in respect of opening of Intern ational Long Distance Service (ILDS) 
to private sector have been receive d and accepted by the government. The 
salient features of the recommendations are enclosed as statement. 
Statement 
Salient features of the recommendations of the TRAI for opening of 
International Long Distance Service to private sector. 
* There is no restriction on the number of players. 
* The applicant company shall have networth of Rs. 25 crores. 
65 

RAJYA SABHA [6 December, 2001] 
* The applicant company shall pay one time Entry Fee of Rs. 25 crores. 
* The annual licence fee shall be 15%  of the Adjusted Gross Revenue 
(AGR). 
* The applicant company sh all submit performance Bank 
Guarantee (BG) of Rs. 25 cror es which will be released on 
fulfilment of the roll out obligations. 
* All bearer services are to be provided by the Licensee. 
* The licence is initially valid for a period of 20 years with automatic 
extension by a period of 5 years subject to satisfactory performance in 
accordance with terms & conditions of the licence particularly in regard to 
Quality of Service (QoS) parameters. 
* International long distance traffic should be routed through National 
Long Distance Operators to the Inte rnational Long Distance Operators 
(ILDOs) gateways for onward transmission to International network. 
* The Licensee will establish a minimum of four gateway switches one in 
each region of the country i.e. Eastern, Western, Northern & Southern within 
three years of signing of licence agreement. 
* Delivery of traffic to all the countries in the World is to be ensured 
through at least four Direct Routes i.e. one each to North America, Gulf 
Region, Europe and any one location in Sourth East Asia, Far East and 
Oceania within three years of signing of licence agreement. 
* Two type of Quality of Service (QoS) are permitted.

Retail Post, Greetings Post, Data Post  etc. Through Business Development

Greeting Post 
The Department launched this novel and unique product Greetings Post in

households and businesses throughout In dia. Corporates, specially the direct 
marketers can be benefited by having select addresses for direct marketing.

launched Speed Post Passport Service on 5th March 2001. The primary 
objective of Speed Post Passport Serv ice is to decentralize the acceptance of

Delay in sporting of mail 
1843. SHRI K. B. KRISHNA MU RTHY: Will the Minister of 
COMMUNICATIONS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Department of Posts conducts National Test Letter Runs 
to test the efficiency of mail sorting and delivery system in metropolitan 
cities; 
(b) if so, whether it was found that almost 50 per cent of the mail was 
delivered late and sorting could not be conducted properly in Chennai, 
Delhi, Hyderabad and Mumbai post offices; and 
(c) whether automatic mail processing systems commissioned in metro 
cities are grossly under-utilised, while extra amount is spent on manual 
sorting? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
COMMUNICATIONS (SHRI TAPAN SIKDAR): (a) The National Test 
Letter Run (NTLR) has been abolished by the Department vide its letter No. 
38-13/99-D dated 15.12.1999 as the NTLR was introduced to assess 
performance of Quick Mail Service which was abolished earlier. The 
Department is however, conducting Live Mail 
90 

[6 December, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
Surveys    to    assess   delivery    efficiency   of   mails    on    a    regular 
basis all over the country. 
(b) No, Sir. As per the results of the Metro Mail Survey 
conducted in September, 2001, th e delivery efficiency of mail 
in Chennai, Delhi, Hyderabad and Mumbai is as follows:— 
Chennai 98.9% 
Delhi 98.5% 
Hyderabad 96.1% 
Mumbai 99.1% 
(c) There are two Letter Sorting Machines (LSMs) each in 
the Automatic Mail Processing Centres (AMPCs) at Mumbai 
and Chennai respectively. Out of the two machines, one is 
kept as standby so that the entire volume of mail is not 
delayed in the event of breakdown. 
The full capacity utilisation of Automatic Mail Processing Centres 
(AMPCs) depends on availability of machinable mails which conform to 
standards of size, length, breadth, thickness, non-use of stapler pin etc. 
Availability of machinable mail thus depends largely on the co-operation of 
the public. Non-availability of sufficient machinable mails is the main reason 
for under utilisation of the AMPCs. The Department is making all possible 
efforts to popularise the concept of machinable mails and educate the public 
in suitably preparing their mails.

1853. PROF. M. SANKARALINGA M: Will the Minister' of 
CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Antyodaya Anna Yojana launched by Government has 
helped in providing highly-subsidised foodgrains to the poorest of the 
poor families in Orissa where starvation deaths have been reported; 
(b) if so, the details of the same; 
(c) the number .of families who fall under such scheme; and 
(d) the States which are implementing this scheme? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI ASHOK 
PRADHAN): (a) Yes, Sir. Antyodaya Anna Yojana (AAY) has helped in 
providing highly subsidized foodgrains to the poorest of the poor families in 
Orissa. 
(b) and (c) AAY envisages identification of 1 crore poorest of the poor 
families in the country and providing them with highly subsidized 
foodgrains @ Rs. 2 a kg. for wheat and Rs. 3 a kg. for rice. The scheme has 
been implemented in the State of Orissa after identification of beneficiaries 
and issue of distinctive cards to 5,05,500 Antyodaya families from 
September, 2001. Government of India is allotting 12,638 MTs of rice per 
month to the State @ 25 kg./family per month for distribution at the retail 
issue price of Rs. 3/- per kg. 
(d) The AAY has been implemented in all States/UTs except Arunachal 
Pradesh, Delhi, Manipur, Lakshadweep and Tamil Nadu where the task of 
identification of Antyodaya families and issue of distinctive ration cards is in 
progress.

Changes in Foodgrains Procurement Policy 
1863. SHRI A. VIJAYA RAGHAVAN: Will the Minister of CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have effected any change in its procurement 
policy of foodgrains; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether any State Governments have supported this programme; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI ASHOK 
PRADHAN):(a) to (d) No, Sir. Under the present policy, Government 
procures all the foodgrains conforming to Fair Average Quality (FAQ) 
specifications through the Food Corporation of India (FCI) and State 
Government Agencies under price sup port operations. However, the farmers 
have the option to sell their produce to FCP/State Government at support 
prices or in the open market, as is advantageous to them. 
However, in order to make the concept of Minimum Support Price a reality 
to all farmers every wher e in the country, the Union Government has been 
persuading States to adopt the scheme  of decentralized procurement. Under 
this scheme, the State Governments would procure, store and distribute food 
grains to meet their requirement for Public Distribution System and other 
welfare schemes. The difference between the economic cost of the State 
118 

[6 December, 2001]        RAJYA SABHA 
Government and Central Issue Price (CIP) is passed on to State Government 
as food subsidy. Government of India would work out a detailed scheme in 
consultation with State Governments to share gains of localized 
procurement. It has been clarified to the States that the scheme would not be 
imposed on any State. The present arrangement would continue where States 
are not yet prepared to shift to a decentralized system of procurement. 
Meetings have been convened with Food Secretaries of Assam, Orissa, 
Bihar, Karnatka, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, West Bengal, Chattisgarh, 
Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Maharashtra and Rajasthan. The Government of 
Assam is willing to implement the scheme. The States were made aware of 
the benefits of decentralized procurement scheme and were asked to submit a 
comprehensive blue print of the proposals required to be addressed, to 
embark on this scheme.

terror" and that another 9000 Jehadis had been waiting to cross the border

Afghanistan against terrorism, because of the extreme international pressure 
that was brought to bear on it, and not out of its own choice. In an address to 
the nation on 19th September, 2001, 
156 

[6 December, 2001] RAJYA SABHA

against terrorism on the grounds that Pakistan had to protect four critical

Centrally Sponsored Schemes 
1926. SHRI KHAGEN DAS:  Will the Minister of LABOUR be pleased 
to state: 
(a) the salient features of the Ce ntrally Sponsored Schemes for 
Rehabilitation of Bonded Labour, Equipment Modernisation and 
Maintenance, Introduction of Trades in  Industrial Training Institute and 
Setting up of new Women's Wing Management Information system, etc.; 
(b) the criteria for allocating funds unde r each scheme to the States and 
corresponding Central share, whether funds are given to the States as 100 per 
cent grant or follow the usual 70/30 (loan/ grant) formula for plan assistance; 
and 
(c) the details of the proposals received, funds released and utilisation for 
the last three years. State-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF LABOUR (SHRI 
MUNI LALL): (a) and (b) The salient features of the Centrally Sponsored 
Schemes are given in Statement-I (See below). 
(c) The State-wise/Scheme-wisc details of the funds released during last 3 
years are given in Statement-II. 
 Statement-I 
Rehabilitation of Bonded Labour: 
Centrally Sponsored Scheme for Rehabilitation of Bonded Labourers is 
being operated since May, 1978. Rehabilitation Assistance to the extent of 
Rs. 20,000/- per freed bonded labourer is provided under the Scheme. The 
expenditure is shared by the Central & State Govt, concerned on 50:50 basis. 
Further, under the modified Centrally Sponsored Scheme, which is effective 
from May, 2000. 100% subsidy is give @ Rs. 2 lakh per district for 
conducting surveys of bonded labourers, Rs. 5 lakh per State per annum for 
conducting evaluatory studies and Rs. 10 lakh per State per annum for 
creating 
175 

RAJYA SABHA [6 December, 2001] 
awareness generation relating to abo lition of bonded labour system. The 
expenditure for conducting surveys, evaluatory studies and awareness 
generation programmes are entirely borne by the Central Government and 
there is no State's share in the expenditure on the above components. 
The Central Assistance are released to States on the receipt of complete 
proposals from the States. 
Equipment Modernization and Maintenance, Introduction of Trades in 
Industrial Training Institute and setting up of new women's wings 
Management Information System: 
1. Equipment Modernization Scheme: The objective of the scheme is to 
assist States/UTs in replacing obsolete and outdated equipments and making 
up shortages in the identified 378 ITIs, so that proper equipment is made 
available for training to work on. The expenditure under this scheme is 
shared on 50:50 basis between Central and Statc-Governments. 
2. Establishment of Equipment Maintenance System: Keeping in view the 
large number of Govt. ITI s spread all over the country and the prevailing 
inadequate maintenance system/situation of machinery, it was proposed to 
set up 19 Equipment Maintenance Workshops and 100 Machine 
Maintenance Cells spread all over the country. The expenditure under this 
scheme is shared on 50:50 basis between Central and State Governments. 
3. Introduction of new trade courses in existing ITI s: The main objective 
of the scheme is to expand existing ITI s adequately by introducing new 
based trades, so that these institu tes are in position to produce skilled 
craftsmen, quantitatively and qualitatively to meet specific demands of 
present and future industries. The expenditure under this scheme is shared on 
50:50 basis between the Central and State Governments. 
4. Establishment of new ITI s/Wings for women: The objective of the 
scheme is to expand the Women's Vocational Training Programme, both 
quantitatively and qualitatively to meet the growing skilled manpower 
requirements for Industry, service sector and self employment. 100 ITI 
s/Wings for women have been set up under the scheme. The expenditure 
under this scheme is shared on 50:50 basis between the Central and State 
Governments. 
176 

[6 December, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
5. Establishment of Management Information System: The main objective of 
the scheme is to improve National Vocational Training System planning, 
management and supervision by establishing Management Information 
System, procurement of computer hard ware and software and setting up of 
MIS units at State Directorates. The scheme envisages training of users in the 
application of software developed by NIC. The scheme is 100% funded by 
the Central Government. 
The funds released during last 3 years under different components of the 
project were fully utilized by the States  and no advance funds were released 
to the States during the period.
